articles.text: The Piedmont Police Department will host its 3rd annual Classic Car Show in the middle of town this Saturday, September 24 from 10 a.m. to 2 p.m. The event is an extension of public events called Coffee, Cars & Cops, and is organized by Officer Tyler Petit. Last year’s Car Show had vehicles lined up on Magnolia and Highland Avenue nearly encircling Piedmont Park. Petit reported yesterday that owners of 91 vehicles have signed up for this year’s show, including a 1929 Ford Model A, 1963 Studebaker Avanti, and a 1987 Ferrari Testarossa. The car show includes free coffee and donuts. In addition, a taco truck will be on hand to feed the masses, and Piedmont teens will sell baked goods. In 2018, its first year, the show had 25 vehicles. Last year the number grew to over 90 vehicles, and Petit is expecting to have more than 100 vehicles this year. Classic and exotic vehicles are especially welcome. Owners who want their cars to be in the show need to register by tomorrow, September 22, on the Eventbrite website: Eventbrite.com/e/coffee-cars-cops-car-show-tickets-348146554717. All cars will be on view on Magnolia Avenue near Piedmont Park. For more information, contact Officer Petit at tpetit@piedmont. ca.gov. Last year’s Piedmont Car Show featured a row of gleaming exotic sports cars in front of the Exedra at Piedmont Park.
articles.title: Annual Classic Car show returns this Sat.

articles.text: Dr. Elise Marks, President of the Association of Piedmont Teachers, encouraged members of the Piedmont School Board at their September 14 meeting to provide a raise for all teachers in part due to a spiraling economy and cost of living. Prior to the meeting, teachers gathered with signs outside of City Hall in a rally urging a pay raise. teachers have taken their message to the streets by coordinating rallies and signs in the mornings during a time when students are dropped off at school. APT is requesting a 7.5% salary increase, plus a one-time bonus pay of $4,000 per full-time member. Inflation and a shortage of teachers drive their requests. Speech by: Dr. Elise Marks, APT President It’s all over the news: the national teacher shortage. Too many classrooms have no teachers. Young people aren’t entering teacher training programs. Mid-career teachers are quitting, often mid-year. Exhausted veteran teachers are retiring early. It’s not just about low wages, but low wages are enough to drive the decision for many. Teacher wages in the US have been flat since 1996, and currently, compared to other professionals with equivalent education, teachers earn 23.5% less–the worst that “wage gap” has ever been. Inflation is pushing teachers over the brink–after a high of 9.1% earlier in the year, inflation was still at 8.3% for August. Prices on most commonly bought groceries are up 30%. This is an emergency. As you know, the problem is especially acute in the Bay Area, where the cost of living is so high the Milpitas school district is asking families to rent rooms out to teachers–like it’s Kansas in 1882, trying to house the schoolmarms, who, of course, were not permitted to have families of their own. This is not a sustainable model for the profession. A generation or so ago, the profession was sustainable. Teachers have never expected to live in luxury, but they were solidly middle class. A teacher could afford a modest home, a modest car. They could afford to have kids, and send those kids to college. Their health insurance was paid in full and they could look forward to a modest but secure retirement. No more. You’ve heard the stories of Piedmont teachers living in uninsulated, mice-infested garages. –Dr. Elise Marks President, Association of Piedmont Teachers Teachers have been wearing their red Association of Piedmont Teachers (APT) shirts every Tuesday this year for awareness of the need for raises. articles.text: Voting website piedmontvotes.com seen as selective Editor: On September 15 a kind neighbor shared a post with me from the private Piedmont Families Facebook group with a group called Piedmont Racial Equity Campaign (PREC) and with a link to a PREC newsletter. In that newsletter, it stated that “PREC as an organization is not making formal endorsements in this election cycle....however, as individual members of the steering committee....we are supporting the following candidates”. It goes on to list Medhekar, Thomasson, Andersen, Long and Ramsey. Within the newsletter, there was a link to a voting website, piedmontvotes.com. Expecting a nonpartisan voting website, I was met with a smear campaign against each of the candidates which PREC did not recommend voting for. This website was clearly created by PREC and was blatantly promotional. My neighbor has yet to hear any of the PREC endorsed candidates or their supporters speak out against chosen a community that would bring itself down to these standards. The PREC website states that they are an organization that “strives to build a thriving community.” I hardly think so. PREC appears to have brought divisive national politicking to the small town of Piedmont. I am new here and this is no way to treat your neighbors who are willing to sacrifice their personal time to run for office. I am especially disturbed that the lone Asian running for school board received the brunt of the attacks. In a climate of Asian hate is this acceptable behavior? Is PREC encouraging Asian attacks against the school board candidate? After seeing this campaign, I will not be voting for any of PREC’s recommended candidates. I will be voting for candidates that stand up for what they believe in rather than candidates that PREC “places” on the City Council and School Board. – Tu Ngoc Nguyen Piedmont resident For 24 years, Piedmont residents have made sure their travels are well documented, with photos of family members reading the Piedmont Post in far-off places throughout the world, and some nearby. articles.text: I was up early on Sunday morning, September 11th. A busy day was ahead. The lead television news stories of the morning were of the motorcade carrying the coffin of Queen Elizabeth II through Scotland and somber observances in New York, Washington DC and Pennsylvania commemorating the 21st anniversary of the terrorist attacks of September 11, 2001. Both stories served as reminders that grief and gratitude are frequent traveling companions. There was an outpouring of grief from people around the globe upon the death of the 96-year-old Queen of England. In Scotland, people lined the roadways as her coffin passed. With the grief there were also many expressions of gratitude for her fidelity to her work, her years as a global leader, her humor and her delight in her four-legged friends. As the motorcade carrying her coffin traversed the Scottish countryside, it was clear that grief and gratitude traveled together. At the sites of the September 11 attacks the dead were remembered, the first responders were honored, hymns were sung, prayers were offered, and speeches were made. All were fitting expressions of the profound grief of that day, the persistent grief that is with us still. Yet, with the grief, there was gratitude. There was gratitude for the courage, the compassion, the connecting which the tragedies evoked. There was gratitude for the rebuilding that has taken place. There was gratitude for the restoration that continues. It was clear that grief and gratitude traveled together. In the biblical narrative, grief and gratitude frequently travel together. In the Psalms, expressions of grief often give way to songs of gratitude. Psalm 74 is an excellent example. This communal prayer originated with the fall of Jerusalem and the destruction of its temple in 586 BCE. The first section (1-11) of complaint and grief is represented by words like “They set fire to your sanctuary, burned it to the ground” (7a). It is followed by a second section (12-17) of gratitude and confidence represented by words like “Yet God has been my king from ancient days” (12a). A lost sheep would have been an occasion for both fear and grief. A caring shepherd would not take such a loss easily or lightly. Jesus then speaks of the joy that comes when the lost is found and the terrified lamb is carried home. When the lost is found there is gratitude. One reason this parable continues to speak, even to those of us unfamiliar with sheep and shepherds, is that most us are well acquainted with loss and grief. articles.text: While cost overruns on public projects are sadly nothing new, the Pool project’s overrun before construction bids have been received and after scope reductions have been made is hard to fathom and extremely disappointing. With that in mind, consider that the City will soon have to face up to the State’s mandate to bring Essential Services Buildings or ESB (police, fire and city offices) up to State code requirements. For comparison, consider that the Pool project is heading toward a $22-23M price tag while the ESB project costs, as compiled by the City Staff in April 2020, was estimated to be between $80 to 100M – and that was with very preliminary plans and scope. Without vastly better methods of cost control for the ESB projects, overruns of the scale of the pool project could easily cause a financial crisis for our small town. A little background. In the lead up to Measure UU, the Pool project was represented as a $15 million project with a $4.5M Contingency added to cover latent conditions, change orders, scope changes, etc. That resulted in the $19.5M Measure UU Bond. The $4.5M Contingency was prudent and warranted given the status of the plans at the time. Now plans have been fully developed (and modified once to reduce the cost) and yet residents are still being asked to fund an additional $2.6M to complete the project. There is also a separate special funding plan seeking $500K to install Heat Pumps to make the project all-electric. So, the project is currently about $3M over budget. If we add the original $4.5M Contingency to the current $3M overage, we have exceeded the original estimate $15M estimate by a whopping $7.5M or 50%. That is quite a miss and underscores my main message: Piedmont must adopt a more rigorous and professional Project Management model. What is that model? It is one where the design team, the project management team and the estimating team all have equal weight and input into the proj-
articles.title: City needs to take Project Management seriously

articles.text: I saw a lawn sign today that read, “Let Us Vote.” This is a fantastic slogan. What upstanding American citizen would oppose voting? But when applied to the issue of housing planning, this approach is deeply flawed. City Council candidates Bridget Harris and Jeanne Solnordal are calling for a citywide vote on the City’s housing plan, even though the City Attorney has stated repeatedly that the proposed zoning changes don’t require a citywide ballot. These candidates claim fiscal responsibility and smart planning. In fact, holding an unnecessary citywide vote would be expensive, counterproductive, and against the City’s interests. To demonstrate this, let’s walk through how such a vote would play out: • First, the City would have to cover the cost of the ballot measure. Unlike the cost of building housing, which is borne by private developers, this would be a public expense of tens of thousands of dollars borne exclusively by Piedmont’s taxpayers. • An election could not be held before the City’s looming deadline to submit its housing plan to the State for approval, so the City would miss the State certification deadline, subjecting Piedmont to a host of penalties. The first penalty is that the City would have one year instead of three years to implement zoning code changes to facilitate housing development, making it extremely difficult for the City to create rational and well-designed zoning requirements that best respond to the community’s needs. With that in mind, consider that the City will soon have to face up to the State’s mandate to bring Essential Services Buildings or ESB (police, fire and city offices) up to State code requirements. For comparison, consider that the Pool project is heading toward a $22-23M price tag while the ESB project costs, as compiled by the City Staff in April 2020, was estimated to be between $80 to 100M – and that was with very preliminary plans and scope. Without vastly better methods of cost control for the ESB projects, overruns of the scale of the pool project could easily cause a financial crisis for our small town. A little background. In the lead up to Measure UU, the Pool project was represented as a $15 million project with a $4.5M Contingency added to cover latent conditions, change orders, scope changes, etc. That resulted in the $19.5M Measure UU Bond. The $4.5M Contingency was prudent and warranted given the status of the plans at the time. Now plans have been fully developed (and modified once to reduce the cost) and yet residents are still being asked to fund an additional $2.6M to complete the project. There is also a separate special funding plan seeking $500K to install Heat Pumps to make the project all-electric. So, the project is currently about $3M over budget. If we add the original $4.5M Contingency to the current $3M overage, we have exceeded the original estimate $15M estimate by a whopping $7.5M or 50%. That is quite a miss and underscores my main message: Piedmont must adopt a more rigorous and professional Project Management model. What is that model? It is one where the design team, the project management team and the estimating team all have equal weight and input into the project from the very early stages. The team needs to avoid iterative design exercises - where a design is completed and then estimated and then often redesigned and estimated again. The design and estimating processes must go forward simultaneously. This management model is not new. It is a model used by most major corporations or entities which have significant building programs. But these are top-down decisions. The Owner, in our case the City Council, must lead and require this model of Project Management if the City hopes to avoid replicating the Pool experience in the future. Regarding the Pool project, it is up to the City Council to establish any accountability for how the Pool project got to where it is. I maintain that the issue is poor project management and definitely not hyperinflation as claimed by some. (Hyperinflation is defined as monthly inflation of 50% or more, and we are not experiencing that.) No, our problem and our issue to resolve is our current method of Project Management. It is not serving us well. We should not and cannot continue to exceed our budgets and then go hat-inhand to our residents to bail out our projects. How Piedmont manages the Pool project moving forward and the ESB projects in the very near future will depend largely on the will of the City Council and City Staff to chart a different path. OPINION 2 campaigns mislead voters on housing Issues By Deborah Leland I saw a lawn sign today that read, “Let Us Vote.” This is a fantastic slogan. What upstanding American citizen would oppose voting? But when applied to the issue of housing planning, this approach is deeply flawed. City Council candidates Bridget Harris and Jeanne Solnordal are calling for a citywide vote on the City’s housing plan, even though the City Attorney has stated repeatedly that the proposed zoning changes don’t require a citywide ballot. These candidates claim fiscal responsibility and smart planning. In fact, holding an unnecessary citywide vote would be expensive, counterproductive, and against the City’s interests. To demonstrate this, let’s walk through how such a vote would play out: • First, the City would have to cover the cost of the ballot measure. Unlike the cost of building housing, which is borne by private developers, this would be a public expense of tens of thousands of dollars borne exclusively by Piedmont’s taxpayers. • An election could not be held before the City’s looming deadline to submit its housing plan to the State for approval, so the City would miss the State certification deadline, subjecting Piedmont to a host of penalties. The first penalty is that the City would have one year instead of three years to implement zoning code changes to facilitate housing development, making it extremely difficult for the City to create rational and well-designed zoning requirements that best respond to the community’s needs. Failure to meet that deadline would lead to escalating penalties, including loss of local control over land use and, potentially, fines. • If a ballot measure is held and the electorate approves the City’s current proposal to allow for additional multifamily housing in certain areas of the City, then we’d be right back where we are today, but at significant cost and detriment to the City, as described above. • If a ballot measure is held and the electorate does not approve the City’s plan to allow additional multifamily housing, then the City will be back at square one in creating a new housing plan to meet State law, while penalties pile up. And, most importantly, if constrained to accommodating multifamily housing in only the limited locations where it is currently allowed, the scale and density of new development that would have to be allowed along Highland Ave. and Grand Ave. would be much greater than what is currently proposed. How is that prudent planning? The promotion of such an untenable proposition by these two City Council candidates is irresponsible and short-sighted, and hardly a model of wise leadership. I urge Piedmonters to confront this reality, and not be fooled by a catchy slogan and an appeal to voter rights. Subscribe!Don’t miss an issue of the paper of Piedmont, by Piedmont, for Piedmont. articles.text: Parents for Educational Excellence in Piedmont (PEEP) is hosting a forum tomorrow for all three candidates running for Piedmont School Board in the November 8 General Election. Candidates running for two open seats on the school board are Ruchi Medhekar, Lindsay Thomasson, and Shirley Hooi. The forum will be held in the Ambassador Chris Stevens Library at Piedmont High School on Thursday, September 22 from 4:30 to 6:30 p.m. Those attending the live event are asked to register in advance at bit.ly/PEEP_Forum. Registrants may submit suggested questions for the candidates. Registered attendees will qualify for raffle prizes. PEEP was founded in 2020 as a 501(c)(4) non-profit organization to connect parents who watch and participate in school board meetings and pay close attention to how decisions affect educational excellence in Piedmont Unified School District. To learn more about the organization, click on EdExcellencePiedmont.com and/or sign up to volunteer.

articles.text: Part two in a series much more likely to apply, and stay, in Piedmont administration and teaching positions. Three candidates are running for two open seats on the Piedmont School Board in the November 8 election. The Piedmont Post will provide extensive coverage on candidates for School Board and for City Council. The Post’s first month of campaign coverage will alternate weekly between City Council and School Board. This week, all School Board candidates were asked to answer the two questions shown below. Due to space limitations, candidates were asked to contain their answers to 150 words per question. QUESTIONS 1. If elected, how would you utilize the ample amount of parent involvement in Piedmont to benefit the schools? 2. PUSD was tasked with finding three new principals and an interim superintendent last summer. What needs to be done to attract and retain top administrators in the district? RUCHI MEDHEKAR 1. Utilizing Parent Involvement Our parent community is an incredible resource and one of the reasons I love living in Piedmont. COVID has provided countless examples of how parents have had to pivot and problem-solve to support their kids’ learning and our schools. I firmly believe that the parent community is an underutilized asset in key ways, which has been frustrating for many of us. We have a remarkable level of expertise which PUSD has leveraged in the past (one example is the Curriculum Forum Committee, which has been inactive since 2014). In other exceptional school districts, there are opportunities for parents to collaborate with their schools to achieve the best decision for students, and we should be open to learning from those models. It is less about parents “getting their way” and more about the integrity of the process, and how (and when) to get buy-in for important decisions. ideas, innovation, and leadership are encouraged, prized, and rewarded. The school board sets the strategy for the district, but it is the superintendent’s role to bring this vision to life. Having a clear and focused direction at the top will help ensure that talent is retained at all levels. SHIRLEY HOOI 1. Utilizing Parent Involvement I applaud the dedication that Piedmont parents have in their volunteer roles across all three school levels and the extraordinary fundraising efforts benefitting the schools. In terms of how to utilize additional parent volunteer time towards the schools, I propose that parents consider utilizing their time to help students directly in strengthening academic outcomes. I envision middle and high school parents stepping into the elementary schools to help the younger students overcome math or reading struggles in order to help create an early love of learning. LINDSAY THOMASSON 1. Utilizing Parent Involvement In my roles as Havens Parent Club President, on the Superintendent Advisory Committee, and in numerous volunteer roles, I’ve experienced firsthand PUSD’s parents’ willingness to give generously of their time, money, and talents, including raising millions of dollars annually for PEF. I value this involvement as one of PUSD’s greatest resources. Yet, many parents voice frustration that they aren’t engaged with the district in meaningful ways. There is not a systematic way for parents to have a seat at the table when decisions regarding new courses, curriculum or hiring occur. I will form district sub-committees that have formal application processes, terms, and responsibilities. They will be subject to the Brown Act so will conduct business in public like the board is required to do. They will ensure stakeholder feedback and buy-in throughout the process. I will also work to increase transparency around administrator hiring processes. 2. Retaining Administrators This year the school board will have the important job of hiring a new superintendent and this person will drive the culture and practices that are critical to attracting and retaining excellent principals. As I know from my experience in building out high-performing teams, a number of important factors play a role in cultivating strong leadership. We must ensure that salaries are in line with the cost of living for all of our district’s employees. We need to cultivate transparency, respect, trust, and open communication. Those foundational elements can move the district to a culture of professionalism where new 2. Retaining Administrators Attracting and retaining qualified teachers and administrators is critical for the success of a school district. With the growing shortage of teachers and administrators nationwide, it is essential that PUSD offers a competitive compensation package and supportive workplace for principals and a superintendent. In retaining principals, it is important for PUSD to provide a rewarding vertical career pathway within PUSD. As for retaining a superintendent, I believe the first step is to hire a superintendent that can achieve PUSD’s set goals. It is not a superintendent’s job to set a district’s goals but rather systematically achieve those goals set by the school board. If the school board lays the road to success for the superintendent, I believe success is a determining factor of retention. 2. Retaining Administrators PUSD should conduct exit surveys of all educators, both administrators and teachers, who depart the district. They must be done in a way that educators feel comfortable responding forthrightly. Responses should be shared with the board and superintendent so we can quickly identify and address concerns, and remedy issues. We also need to have robust conversations with all stakeholders to determine our community priorities. What are our goals for our students when they graduate from our schools? Our collective values as they relate to education? When we can articulate these goals, we can hire administrators who support them, and in turn can support our administrators in achieving our collective objectives. The first notice of a cancellation came at 7:32 p.m. on Friday evening in a message from Jazz Festival coordinator Greg Slatoff notifying the bands scheduled to play that the music portion of the festival had been canceled. The city historically sets up a large stage in the Main Park with a sound system and a piano for the performers. “It is with the greatest disappointment that I must tell you the Jazz Festival has been canceled due to the impeding rain. Issues related to the erection of the stage and maintenance of sound/ electronic systems in wet weather were the factors that prompted the City’s decision,” his message read. The City followed with its own message at 9:53 p.m. “After much deliberation and hoping for a change in the impending storm’s arrival, the City of Piedmont has made the difficult decision to cancel all outdoor activities for Sunday’s Harvest Festival. The weather forecast predicts significant rain and wind gusts starting early Sunday morning and through the early afternoon.” The City has not indicated why alternate sites were not used for some of the festival’s components, to include Scarecrow Alley, Farmer’s Market, Kids’ Carnival and art show. No mention has been made of the availability of the high school gym or its auditorium, the three elementary school auditoriums, or the Staff Photos A rain gauge, with artificially collected water, in the foreground of Piedmont Park. Guild Hall at Piedmont Community Church. The Harvest Festival Committee met late Friday afternoon to discuss the possibility of hosting the event given the impending storm, which was projected to bring half an inch of rain on Sunday. The actual amount of rain was considerably less than the half inch projected. “Staff considered possible alternatives for the Jazz Festival, however moving indoors was not feasible,” said Recreation Department Director Chelle Putzer. The Harvest Festival, which normally attracts 800-1000 attendees, requires the service of dozens of vendors, musicians, students, artists, staff, and volunteers. Three days before the event, on Thursday, September 15, the Piedmont Education Foundation, which helps with the kid’s carnival and scarecrows, sent out a newsletter saying the event would continue “rain or shine.” The optimistic sentiment was not enough, however. articles.text: Last summer, a cohort of Chabot’s Galaxy Explorer high school students worked at NASA’s Ames Research Center in Silicon Valley as part of a larger partnership between NASA Ames and Chabot Space & Science Center. As full-time interns they were placed in departments for project work and close mentorship by NASA staff. Students were paired with scientists and staff based on their interests and For 3-year Galaxy Explorer Sage Mosley, the passion for space began at a young age. She began exploring the cosmos with a Planet Project at age nine, continuing on to Space Camp during middle school for two summers at the U.S. Space and Rocket Center in Alabama, and continuing her internship at Chabot Space & Science Center, which she started as a freshman at Piedmont High School. –Sage Mosley, Chabot Galaxy Explorer and NASA Aeromechanics Intern Piedmont High School senior Sage Mosley is in her fourth year as an intern at Chabot Space & Science “In 3rd grade, I told my parents I wanted to work for NASA,” said Mosley, “Eight years later, I was reading my offer letter to intern at Ames Research Center. I started jumping up and down, and I immediately ran to share the news. My family and friends were beyond proud.” Now as a high school senior, Mosley plans to study Aerospace A photo of the eight Galaxy Explorer interns from Chabot Space & Science Center in Oakland. Engineering in college, with the ultimate goal is of becoming a NASA astronaut. “The most exciting thing about the internship is meeting people with the same passions. While I was nervous to be the youngest in the room on my first day, I was welcomed into a super friendly environment at Ames. Through my example, I hope to encourage others my age to follow their dreams and keep going until they succeed.” Mosley was one of eight Galaxy Explorers interning at NASA Ames last summer. The interns learned directly from mentors in the field, working on projects in supercomputing, data analytics, rotorcraft aeromechanics, lunar missions, public engagement, computer science and STEM engagement. articles.text: You’ve heard teachers talk about how they have to take second jobs at night and on weekends to pay their bills, and how they’re maxing out their credit cards to survive. You’ve heard young teachers tell you how they cannot afford to have children of their own. In the 23 years I have worked in Piedmont, teacher wages have consistently fallen below inflation, and not just because our salary increases haven’t kept pace. Health insurance is another huge piece of the problem. As of 2008, our health insurance in Piedmont was fully paid by the district. In the economic downturn of that year, to help the district maintain all its programs, teachers agreed to take on paying part of our own premiums. The district promised that as the economic picture improved, we’d try to restore some of those benefits. It hasn’t gone that way. As of January– with the cost of Kaiser climbing yet again–I personally will be paying the equivalent of 10% of my take-home pay every month for health insurance. That’s an effective 10% pay cut right there over what I earned just a few years ago. Some local districts–like Oakland and Lafayette–have returned to paying full health benefits for their teachers. Others have significantly raised the caps for the amount of the premium they cover. The maximum health benefit for a Piedmont teacher is $19,800, as it has been for several years. So just under $20,000. San Ramon, which has about the same maximum salary we have, covers $26,493. Acalanes, $27,000. Moraga, $26,700. Albany, $25,169. Martinez, a notoriously low-paying district, covers $27,000; $7,000 a year more than Piedmont. And our maximum salaries are falling behind. As I said last time, one teacher we lost during the summer had four local offers each more than $30,000 a year over what Piedmont pays. How can we hold on to our teachers when our salaries and benefits can’t compete with districts all around us? I’m hearing that Piedmont teachers are getting cold-called.– in September, when the school year has already started – by other desperate local districts looking to poach them right now from Piedmont, offering hiring bonuses of $6000 to $10,000, not to mention higher overall benefits and pay. Almost daily, teachers pull me aside or email me asking, “Do you think we’ll settle soon? Will we get what we’re asking for? I need to decide whether to start sending out my resumé.” In negotiations, APT is asking for a 7.5% salary increase, plus some one-time bonus money – $4,000 per full-time member – to help us recover from the hard hit of inflation. It is estimated to be costing the average Bay Area household an extra $4,400 in 2022. We need [a raise] to make a dent in some of those maxed out credit cards. This ask is relatively modest, given rampant inflation. Most other local teacher unions are asking for increases of between 10-12%. L.A. Unified is asking for 20%, and frankly, that’s the kind of number needed to actually make this profession sustainable. Remember: given where inflation is this year, 7.5% will still be an effective pay cut for Piedmont teachers. Piedmont Unified can afford to give us what we’re asking. Not only does the district have about 3.5 million dollars more than we thought when the budget was approved in June (when APT was offered an average 5% salary increase), it seems clear that with the numbers of veteran teachers we’ve had retiring or resigning, and who are being replaced with much newer teachers, payroll expenses have been dropping dramatically. I’ve been arguing for several years that this savings was coming, as we have a very large number of teachers currently at the highest [level] on our salary schedule, most of whom are planning to retire soon – this year, next year, in another year or two beyond that. Few are planning to stay for another five years. That wave of retirements has been looming for years and is about to break. And indeed, last year when we negotiated a 2.5% raise, we were told at the bargaining table that the district could not afford the raise. Unified is asking for 20%, and frankly, that’s the kind of number needed to actually make this profession sustainable. As you see in the budget presentation tonight, the actual cost has turned out to be…$78,000. I want to make sure everyone hears that. Not $527,000, but $78,000 – difference of almost $450,000 in the district’s financial favor. That savings will keep happening. Because veteran teachers will keep leaving in higher numbers each year. The district office hasn’t even had the chance yet to calculate the impact of the record 18 teachers who left the district this past spring. The rate will be faster or slower depending on what Piedmont does with salary right now, but the net effect will be the same: the district will have more and more money left over with which they can raise teacher pay, and hopefully retain the teachers they still have. articles.text: Two weeks ago, my 6-yearold daughter was all set to do a fun art project. She was going to make an animal pet rock. In front of her was a pile of small rocks to select from, acrylic paints, googly eyes and some bit of fake fur. She was super excited and we started thinking about what kind of animal she would make. All of a sudden, her entire mood changed. Her eyes filled with tears and she curled into a little ball and she looked up at me and said, “Mommy, I’m just so scared it won’t be perfect.” My heart breaks. We talk it through with some really challenging questions: • Why do we make art? • What does “perfect” look like? • Why do you want “perfect”? • If your fear was a creature, what would it look like? • Can we make friends with your fear? Eventually, she came around to a lesson that she had learned in kindergarten: “Perfect doesn’t exist.” She took a deep breath, chose a rock and spent the next hour making a perfectly imperfect Hummingbird pet rock. She was smiling and happy during the process and proud of the outcome which she gave to her grandma as a present. But this whole episode really made me reflect on the power that the concept of “perfect” holds over so many of us. Kids and Why do we make art? adults alike, we can completely knock out entire categories of activities for fear that we won’t do it perfectly. But the creative process is just that, a process. In the end, the outcome is only the sum total of a number of tiny steps. So, how can we ask ourselves for perfection? We can’t control every single tiny step we take. And the joy of the experience of creating is in finding the fun and flow in each of those steps. What creative act would you try if you had no fear of failing? What would your kids want to explore if there was no expectation to be “good” at it? The act of creation is an act of courage because it is putting our own inner self out in the world in some capacity. Most of us didn’t have a kindergarten teacher who taught us that there is no such thing as perfect, so we need to teach ourselves and our kids that it’s ok to be scared and it’s ok to try and it’s ok to just see what happens. When it comes to creativity, it’s not about the destination, it’s about appreciating and enjoying the journey. .Nina Meehan is the CEO and Founder of Bay Area Children’s Theatre, currently performing “Elephant and Piggie: We are in a Play.” For tickets see www.bactheatre.org.
articles.title: The fear of not being perfect

articles.text: A rafting trip is one of the most iconic Scout outings. In addition to being thrilling, it also offers a unique experience and is so much fun. The Scouts weren’t the only ones screaming and laughing; the adult advisors had their share of fun too. After a three-hour drive to Lotus, a tiny town in El Dorado County, the Scouts piled out of the cars into an unbearable heat. After lunch we got our helmets, life jackets and paddles and headed to the American River where we received important safety lessons. We were all baking in the heat, so we were glad to get our feet wet as we waded into the water and climbed into the rafts. After about 10 minutes on the water, we hit the first rapid – not a huge one, but a slightly calmer class II rapid called Swimmers Rapid. Some of us jumped out of the raft and enjoyed a quick dip in the river. This was followed by a string of class II and a few class III rapids. Our guide was wonderful, pointing out the unique rocks and the names given to them, such as Rabbit Rock and Crocodile Rock. I think that “screaming right turn” was one of my favorites. It looked harmless, but there was a reason it was called a “screaming” right turn, believe me. After about an hour and a half of rafting, something worthy of documentation happened – a Scout was tossed out of the boat. He quickly resurfaced and was pulled back into the raft, but became the talk of the trip (which is why I’m including it here. There would be consequences if I didn’t.) At about the same time we stopped for a snack and turned a raft upside down by standing on it with a rope and toppling backwards. What was the purpose? To create a water slide! The line of Scouts wanting to take turns on the slide quickly formed and stretched forever. It was so much fun to plunge into the water endlessly and cool off from the earlier heat. After the break I had more sand and water in my shoes than ever and was soaked. There were more class III rapids for the second part of the trip and several people claimed they were tossed upside down. After an epic race to the end of the run at Folsom Lake, 10 miles downstream from where we started, we climbed into the bus with a cold drink and returned to the Mother Lode campground, a mere 18 minutes away. With every step we left behind sopping footprints that almost immediately evaporated in the dry heat. After washing our gear we found our campsite and set up. Most of the Scouts chose to sleep under the stars, but a friend and I wanted some protection from the elements, so we grabbed a tent – only to discover it had no poles. Luckily Scoutmaster Cantrill was kind enough to lend us his tent, an example of one of the points of the Scout Law– kindness. That made my day. He was willing to give up his tent to a pair of Photos courtesy of Mother Lode rafting Piedmont Scouts on a rafting trip on the American River.

He quickly resurfaced and was pulled back into the raft, but became the talk of the trip (which is why I’m including it here. There would be consequences if I didn’t.) At about the same time we stopped for a snack and turned a raft upside down by standing on it with a rope and toppling backwards. What was the purpose? To create a water slide! The line of Scouts wanting to take turns on the slide quickly formed and stretched forever. It was so much fun to plunge into the water endlessly and cool off from the earlier heat. After the break I had more sand and water in my shoes than ever and was soaked. There were more class III rapids for the second part of the trip and several people claimed they were tossed upside down. After an epic race to the end of the run at Folsom Lake, 10 miles downstream from where we started, we climbed into the bus with a cold drink and returned to the Mother Lode campground, a mere 18 minutes away. With every step we left behind sopping footprints that almost immediately evaporated in the dry heat. After washing our gear we found our campsite and set up. Most of the Scouts chose to sleep under the stars, but a friend and I wanted some protection from the elements, so we grabbed a tent – only to discover it had no poles. Luckily Scoutmaster Cantrill was kind enough to lend us his tent, an example of one of the points of the Scout Law– kindness. That made my day. He was willing to give up his tent to a pair of Photos courtesy of Mother Lode rafting Piedmont Scouts on a rafting trip on the American River. E v e n t C a l e n d a r By Jay Russell Museum of Art and Digital Entertainment (MADE) Themade.org 921 Washington St, Oakland 350-8857 Video Game Museum The MADE is a non-profit museum preserving video game culture and offering real hands-on video game play on site. It is the world’s first and only all-playable video game museum, inspiring the next generation of game developers. Play thousands of games on original hardware and check out one-of-a-kind pieces of gaming history. The MADE is open Wednesday-Sunday, and stays open late until 9:00 p.m. on Friday and Saturday. Piedmont Ballet Piedmontballetacademy.com 1333 Grand Avenue, Piedmont, 350-8375 Aspiring and continuing ballet dancers starting at age four can receive dancing lessons at Piedmont Ballet Academy on Grand Ave, in Piedmont. Drop-in classes are available and dancers can still join in the fall session at a prorated cost. Piedmont Ballet values traditional technique but also gentle, progressive teaching, body type and racial inclusivity, and community. Performance opportunities include The Nutcracker in December and an annual recital at Holy Names University in the spring. Learn the positions, traditional exercises, and all the locomotor movements that will evolve into more complex steps as training advances. Blackhawk Museum Blackhawkmuseum.org 3700 Blackhawk Plaza Circle, Danville (925) 736-2280 Classic Car Showroom and Natural History Museum This museum is well worth the 25-mile drive to Danville. The most popular exhibit of the museum may well be its collection of classic and rare cars. Kids will see not only a showroom with more than 100 near priceless cars, but a showroom on the top floor with incredible one-of-akind vehicles. Marvel at an 1886 Benz Patent Motorwagen, the first gas powered vehicle, and the 1967 Shelby Mustang GT500 “Eleanor” from the movie Gone in 60 Seconds. Not to be missed re the natural history museum exhibits at Blackhawk, including “Into Africa,” “Spirit of the Old West,” and “Into China.” Oakland Zoo Oaklandzoo.org 9777 Golf Links Rd, Oakland 632-9525 Visit the Oakland Zoo to hang out with all the fuzzy and ferocious animals that will have the whole family wow-ed. The Zoo is celebrating its 100th anniversary and is open every day from 10:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. The Zoo’s gondola delivers kids and their adult companions to the amazing boardwalk of the California Trail, for viewings of wolves, buffalo and bears. The skyride and amusement rides are open for fun as well. 12-year-old girls so that we could be comfortable. I am so lucky to know such wonderful people and be able to experience such amazing things. Huge thanks to Mother Lode rafting for helping us all the wayfrom guiding us on the rafts to telling us the name of the rapids to helping us clean our gear, they were truly amazing. Samantha Pell is a member of Piedmont Scout Council’s Troop One who still has water and sand in her boots. Floating down the American River in the fall.

articles.text: Girl Scout project by Wildwood alum benefits everyone On September 1, an estimated 200 students at Wildwood Elementary School took action and walked, scootered and biked to school. The event was the idea of Piedmont High senior Skye Yeh, a Wildwood alum, as part of her Girl Scout Gold Award. During the summer she and some helpers built three new scooter racks which now reside in the school courtyard. The idea came after seeing the over-crowded drop off and pick ups in front of the school. Too many cars have created unsafe situations for the students. After talking with Wildwood Principal Carol Cramer, and a safety officer at Piedmont Police, Skye decided she wanted to get more cars off the streets. A list of reasons for students to participate in the Walk and Roll event was compiled and shared with students, teachers and parents; along with some safety rules. The school had almost 78% of students walk, scooter, bike and even one who roller skated to school. The classes ranged from a 95% participation to a 61% participation. The street in front of the school was noticeably emptier that morning. The teachers were thankful for the scooter racks and for the event and hope for a continued habit of choosReasons to walk or scoot to school • It’s Fun. Walking and scootering are more fun than sitting in a car. • It’s Healthy. Exercise is good for your body. • It’s a great way to start the day. Exercise gets your brain going, too. • It’s planet friendly. Fewer cars means less pollution. • It’s friendly. Walking with neighbors makes new friends • It’s safer. Fewer cars make safer streets. Safety rules when walking to school • Stay on sidewalks • Use crosswalks • Walk with friends and neighbors • Look both ways before crossing a street and wait for cars to stop • Be aware of your surroundings, especially near driveways • Listen to crossing guards and police officers Safety rules when riding a scooter to school • Wear a properly fitting helmet • Adjust your scooter to a proper and safe height • Be mindful of pedestrians and alert them you are near • Follow all walking rules • Ride on the sidewalk, not in the street • Use the new racks at school to store your scooter and helmet • Remember to take your helmet and scooter home at the end of the day Skye Yeh and Nikila Rao building a rack. Skye Yeh and Carol Cramer stand by the newly installed racks. Skye attaching hardware. ing self-propelled transportation over cars. ”I’m so proud of all the students who biked or scootered to school or found a way to walk The new scooter rack being used. instead of being driven,” said Wildwood Principal Carol Cramer. Skye commented that she hopes students and parents learned something or felt empowered to make a difference in their future choices that affect their safety, health and the health of the environment. Walkers Nora and Julio Montes with Izzy and Greg Wheeler. The unusually empty drop off area during event. Sarah scootering to school. The overflowing bike racks at Wildwood school.

articles.text: Due to the threat of rain on Sunday, September 18, the city of Piedmont made the decision at 9:53 p.m. on Friday, September 16, to cancel nearly the entire multi-faceted annual event scheduled for Sunday in Piedmont Park from 11 a.m. to 4 p.m. The lone survivor was the Edible Food Contest, a mainstay of the Festival since its first year. With 127 entries of homemade jams, jellies, breads, and pickles, the contest turned the Community Center into a large array of produce and baked goods displaying the bounty of Piedmont cooks and gardeners, Founded in 1998 by Bill Drumm and former mayor Susan Hill, the Festival itself is a sixring circus, with a jazz festival, Kids’ Carnival, Farmers Market, art exhibit, and Scarecrow Alley – a large collection of life-sized scarecrows made primarily by school kids. And the Edible Food Contest. Categories of foods in recent years have included curds, pies, pesto, and cookies, and a prize for the biggest zucchini and most unusual vegetable. With 127 entries of homemade jams, jellies, breads, and pickles, the contest turned the Community Center into a large array of produce and baked goods displaying the bounty of Piedmont cooks and gardeners, Founded in 1998 by Bill Drumm and former mayor Susan Hill, the Festival itself is a sixring circus, with a jazz festival, Kids’ Carnival, Farmers Market, art exhibit, and Scarecrow Alley – a large collection of life-sized scarecrows made primarily by school kids. And the Edible Food Contest. Categories of foods in recent years have included curds, pies, pesto, and cookies, and a prize for the biggest zucchini and most unusual vegetable. See Food Contest on page 32 The Vitter family shares a laugh with Greg Slatoff (right). Staff photo Staff photo Katia, Anastasia, and Sasha Lindgardt, winners of growing the largest zucchini. Staff photo The Vitter family had relatives visiting from Vienna during the Harvest Festival. THE BEST CARE FOR YOUR BEST FRIEND If you’re looking for the best in veterinary care, come to The Grand Lake Veterinary Hospital for personalized, compassionate care. Our state-of-the-art facility is locally owned and operated, and we are known for providing extraordinary, individualized care to our patients. It’s the heart of our commitment to a long-term investment in our community. (510) 327-1325 | GRANDLAKEVET.COM 3331 GRAND AVE, OAKLAND, CA 94610 Harvest Festival Edible Contest results – 2022 Piedmont’s popular Edible Food Contest bounced back to life in full form last Sunday, with more entrants than last year and ribbons awarded to folks from age 5 to 85. Jovie Strzelecki, who had never entered the contest before, walked off with the Bill Drum Award for the most blue ribbons. “It was a true community event. articles.text: In a one-sided affair, Piedmont’s boys’ water polo team dominated San Leandro, 21-3, at the Pirates’ home pool on Tuesday, September 13. Piedmont remains undefeated with a 5-0 record. The Highlanders finished the night with 12 different players scoring, led by Declan Linnane, Finn Burke, and Hayden Jahn each with. A hat trick (3 goals). Notably, Jahn was just called up from the junior varsity team. Piedmont led 8-3 by the end of the first quarter and 14-3 at halftime. The Highlanders extended the gap to 16-3 in the third quarter and closed off with five more goals in the final period. In the first quarter, Peter Krumins scored the opening goal after barely one minute. San Leandro quickly tied after 17 seconds, but Finn Burke scored just 12 seconds later to put the Highlanders ahead 2-1, a lead they never relinquished. Burke scored once more with 5:02 left in the first just eight seconds after drawing a man-advantage, 3-1, followed by three quick goals by Linnane, Farris Saffouri, and Daniel Banin in the next minute to make it 6-2 with 3:31 left. San Leandro made it 6-3 with 3:03 left in the quarter but Evan Dickason and George Stein answered with goals at 1:29 and 1:01 for a Piedmont 8-3 lead.. Piedmont added six unanswered goals in the second quarter. It took just 18 seconds for PHS to score in the second quarter when Linnane sent one in. Krumins then made it 10-3 after 30 seconds. A minute later, Charlie Wright netted one and just 20 seconds later Jahn made it 12-3. With 2:10 left in the second, Linnane made it 13-3 and Evan Dickason sent one in with just four Photos by Nancy Brahm Declan Linnane scored three goals, and had an assist and three steals against San Leandro. ticks left. In the third, the Highlanders added two goals from Jahn with 5:33 and 4:28 left in the quarter. The. Highlanders scored five more times in the last period. Leo Hurwitz scored 50 seconds into the quarter and then Burke put in another goal 40 seconds later. With 2:26 remaining, Ori Aloush scored two goals, and Hurwitz scored the final goal with 15 seconds left on the clock. Final stats: Linnane scored three goals, one assist, and three steals. Burke scored three, one assist, and two steals. Jahn had three goals as well. Dickason and Aloush scored twice and had an assist. Krumins had two goals and an assist. Hurwitz scored once and had three steals. Kreickhaus had a goal, assist, and steal. Wright, Stein, and Banin had a goal and assist. Saffouri had an individual goal. NEXT UP Piedmont (5-0 overall, 1-0 league) takes on rival Berkeley on the road today, Wednesday, September 22 for a 5:00 p.m. match. The following two days, PHS competes in a tournament at Napa Valley College on September 23-24. Finn Burke had three goals, an assist, and two steals. Peter Krumins scored two goals and had an assist.

articles.text: 3-0 loss to O’Dowd, 3-0 win vs. Encinal The PHS girls’ volleyball team split its last two matches, defeating Encinal 3-0 on Monday, September 19 at Binks Rawlings Gym (25-16, 28-26, 25-17) and losing 3-0 to Bishop O’Dowd on Wednesday, September 14. The victory over the Jets on Monday snapped a three-match losing streak after playing Skyline, Berkeley, and O’Dowd. “I’m glad we’re getting our feet in the water and testing different things. We’re trying out a different rotation/ We’re trying to figure out what our best rotation is,” said coach Mariah Cardenas. It was a strong night for junior outside hitter Sadie Town, who led the team with 11 kills. “She got fed a lot, and she’s a really smart player in terms of placement. Sadie has been playing club [volleyball] for a long time. She’s only a junior, so we’re happy to get her for another year. She’s really strong and has a great swing,” explained Cardenas. 3-0 win over Encinal In the first set, the two sides traded points until Piedmont held a 7-6 lead, which started an eight point scoring run for the Highlanders to make it 15-6. The two sides exchanged possessions over Piedmont’s final 10 points until winning 25-16, closing with a service error by Encinal. The teams traded points all the way until the closing moments of the second set, finishing with PHS claiming their second set-win to go ahead 2-0. Encinal came out with a 3-0 lead in the second set, but PHS clawed back until gaining a 7-6 lead—which included kills by Town, Tara Kothari, and Shelby Cavenaugh during the run. The sides dueled until PHS held set-point at 24-23 but a defensive error kept the Jets alive. At 26-26, Kothari slammed a kill for the 27th point followed by an offensive error by Encinal to solidify PHS’ win. Encinal similarly jumped out to a 3-0 advantage in the third set, but PHS came back to tie at 3-3 and they traded points until the set was at 8-8. But from there, Piedmont claimed the lead at 9-8 and never looked back, claiming Staff Photos Sadie Town had a big game with 11 kills and two aces against Encinal. Tara Kothari had a strong performance with five kills against Encinal. the next 10 of 12 points to go ahead 19-10. After a small run by the Jets, Piedmont led 20-15, but the Highlanders closed out by winning the next five of seven points with several errors by Encinal. Final stats: Town had 11 kills and two aces. Elena Stevens had three blocks. Kothari had five kills, Bree DeYoung had four kills, and Shelby Cavenaugh had three. 3-0 loss to Bishop O’Dowd The Dragons are still one of the strongest volleyball programs in the Bay Area, They have won 10 consecutive Western Alameda County Conference championships since joining the league in 2012. They lost just once against league opponents during the current span, which was in 2016 against San Leandro. BOD won last Wednesday’s match by scores of 25-15, 25-14, and 25-11. Final stats were not provided. NEXT UP Piedmont (6-6 overall, 2-2 league) heads to Castro Valley today, Wednesday, September 21, for a 7:00 p.m. match. They also face El Cerrito at the Gauchos home gym on Saturday, September 24 at 10:00 a.m. Elena Stevens (11) had three blocks against the Jets.

articles.text: Staff Photos Anne Jumper won at No. 1 singles in straight sets over Bentley, 6-1, 6-0. Cecilia DeFazio paired with Emma Eisemon at No. 1 doubles for a decisive 6-2, 6-2 win. Piedmont’s girls’ tennis team had a cakewalk with Bentley on Tuesday, September 13. Playing at home, the Highlanders rolled to a 6-1 victory, including three matches that were shutous. “We had a solid day with several shutout double-bagel (6-0, 6-0) wins. We won all of our matches in straight sets,” said Piedmont coach Jim Landes. Playing No. 1 singles, Anne Jumper won handily, 6-1, 6-0. Carolina Romanczuk pitched a shutout No. 2, 6-0, 6-0, as did Ellie Broscow at No. 3. The only loss on the day was at No. 2 singles with Annika Gilliland falling 6-3, 6-0. It marked Jumper’s fourth win of the season and Romanczuk’s fifth. The match was Broscow’s first appearance in the singles lineup after playing two doubles matches earlier this season. In doubles, Emma Eisemon and Cecilia DeFazio paired at the No. 1 spot for another easy win, 6-2, 6-2. Kate Jumper and Arianna Kortum combined for a 6-0, 6-1 win at No. 2 doubles, and Asha Byers and Abigail Call recorded another double-bagel at No. 3, winning 6-0, 6-0. Freshmen Kate Jumper and Kortum, are making a solid start on the varsity roster, marking their second win as a pair. Emma Eisemon and DeFazio, a strong pairing in 2021, have moved into the No. 1 doubles role. They have won twice as a tandem, and have appeared in the top slot in several big matches. “They may be our top doubles team,” said Landes. “We could move around some singles players, but they were great last season,” The Highlanders look ahead to league opponents Castro Valley tomorrow, September 22 at the Trojans’ home courts. It will be Piedmont’[s fourth match in the Western Alameda County Conference, where it is undefeated at 3-0. Piedmont currently looks like the best team in the WACC after defeating last year’s champions, Bishop O’Dowd, 5-2 at the California Tennis Classic in Fresno on September 10. Tuesday vs. Lick Wilmerding Piedmont traveled to San Francisco on Tuesday, September 20, to take on North Coast Section power Lick Wilmerding. See next week’s Post for match details. NEXT UP Piedmont (5-3 overall, 3-0 league) heads to Castro Valley on Thursday, September 22. for a 3:30 p.m. Freshman Arianna Kortum won at No. 2 doubles, with Kate Jumper, 6-0, 6-1.

articles.text: With a scheduled early-season Senior Night on Tuesday, September 13, Piedmont’s girls’ water polo team ran roughshod over San Leandro at Pirates’ home pool, 14-3. A ceremony honored the team’s five seniors: Rosie Feldman, Odessa Dando, Annika Nilsson, Macie Gard, and Molly Ashton. Coach Sarah Mooney had high praise for each of them. “Rosie has been a major contributor for many years, same with Odessa these last four years, while Annika has been the backbone of our defense. Macie’s growth has allowed her to understand every position in the pool. Molly’s mental toughness and fighter mentality is huge asset that inspires the team,” said coach Mooney. PHS led 5-0 by the end of the first quarter and 10-1 by halftime. Piedmont started the fourth quarter leading 13-3 and scored once more in the fourth for the 14-3 final. It took only 10 seconds for Piedmont to score its first goal. Dando won the opening sprint, leading to Katerina Melian scoring on a shot from distance. Dando made it 2-0 at the 5:30 mark in close distance on a breakaway opportunity. Thirty seconds later, PHS Macie Gard (left) is honored by coach Sarah Mooney in a postgame ceremony for seniors. Kate Meyjes had two goals for Piedmont against San Leandro. Photos by Nancy Brahm Piedmont honored their five seniors on the roster during Senior Night on Tuesday, September 13. Pictured are: Rosie Feldman (left), Molly Ashton, Odessa Dando, and Annika Nilsson. (Not pictured, Macie Gard.) drew an exclusion to gain a man-advantage, leading to Ashton scoring after 12 seconds of time on the penalty, making it 3-0. Ashton scored once more with 4:14 left in the quarter after an assist by Dando, while Gard made it 5-0 with 2:09 remaining on a long pass from Feldman. In the five-goal second quarter, Kate Meyjes scored after two minutes when Alicia Bernales sent in a pass in front of the net. With 3:46 left in the half, Meyjes scored again after recovering a loose ball for a 7-0 lead. With 1:56 on the clock, Sonja ten Grotenhuis scored on an assist by goalie Friedie Schickedanz – a nice gift on ten Grotenhuis’ birthday. Anne Reardon made it 9-0 for Piedmont after Sage Gilbert sent an assist with 40 seconds left. The Pirates scored with 22 seconds left to make it 9-1 but Sydney Olson scored for PHS with 12 seconds remaining on a ten Grotenhuis assist, for a 10-1lead. Piedmont scored three times in the third period and allowed the Pirates two goals with substitutions in the water, San Leandro scored after two minutes, but Vivian Burke answered a minute later, making it 11-2. With 3:33 left, Melian sent a pass to Bernales in close distance for the goal, 12-2. Olson scored with 1:30 left in the third after rebounding her own penalty shot off the crossbar. The Pirates added a goal with 1:15 left in the quarter. In the fourth quarter, Piedmont killed an early penalty opportunity for San. Leandro in the first minute of action with the help of Gard, now playing as goalie. The Highlanders scored the only goal in the fourth when Feldman netted one with 3:37 left in the game. Final stats: Meyjes, Ashton, and Olson also scored twice. Feldman, Melian, ten Grotenhuis, Bernales, and Dando each scored once and had an assist. Gard, Burke, and Reardon had individual goals. Schickedanz and Gilbert had assists. Tuesday vs. Marin Academy The Highlanders were scheduled to play Marin Academy in San Rafael yesterday, Tuesday, September 21. See next week’s Post for match details. NEXT UP Piedmont (2-3 overall, 1-1 league) heads to Berkeley today, Wednesday, September 21 for a 5:45 p.m. match.

articles.text: Piedmont’s football team suffered a 56-35 loss to Pierce in Arbuckle on Friday, September 16. It was the team’s third straight loss. The Highlanders fought evenly with the Bears in the first half and went into halftime down by one touchdown, 28-21, but Pierce ate away at the Purple and White defense with continuous running plays to charge ahead in the second half on Piedmont’s tired legs with a roster of only 17 players. “We were going back-andforth in the first half and just couldn’t get any stops in the second half. We shot ourselves in the foot a couple of times, but we put up some good points and played hard,” said coach Jordan Seiden. “The battle with attrition is always going to be an issue for us. Our core group is great, but it’s a lot to ask them to play all four quarter both ways. Pretty much every single player starts both ways. We ask a lot of them and they’ve been great about it.” The Bears rushed for over 500 yards and only attempted a few passes, accumulating 32 first downs on the night with successive long drives, including four of five fourth-down conversions. “We did pretty good on third downs, but they converted multiple fourth downs,” said Seiden. “They just ran the ball, but we did well stopping the inside run but lost discipline on a lot of outside runs,” said Seiden. Piedmont started the game off with a bang on a trick play when running back Jack Nelson took a sweep and tossed the ball to receiver Sam Shelby running a reverse. Shelby, who is the backup quarterback, pulled up to pass and hit DominIc Alexander wide open downfield for a 62-yard touchdown. Pierce responded on its next series with a touchdown drive to make it 7-7. But the Highlanders were able to regain the lead on a 60-yard pass reception by Shelby. On the play, quarterback Markos Lagios connected with Shelby on an eight-yard buttonhook. The receiver then shook off two defenders and raced down the sideline, making another two defenders whiff on tackles as he sped to the end zone. Pierce scored the next two touchdowns with its Wing-T offense, churning out rushing yards on long drives to go ahead Photos by Mike McConathy Dominic Alexander scored twice against Pierce on pass receptions of 62 and 25 yard receptions. Matteo Costa scored on an 86-yard kickoff return against Pierce. Sam Shelby had a 62-yard touchdown pass on a trick play and also turned multiple defenders inside-out on a 60-yard touchdown reception. 21-14 in the early portion of the second quarter. But Piedmont answered with an 86-yard kickoff return for a touchdown by Matteo Costa to tie the game once more at 21-21 Pierce added one more touchdown before the half for a 28-21 lead, and Piedmont struggled to find productivity in the second half. “I firmly appreciate the effort they give for all four quarters. To ask them to play as much as they do, I have nothing but the utmost love for these players. But it can’t be an excuse for the mental mistakes we make,” said Seiden. The Bears scored two more unanswered touchdowns in the third quarter to make it 42-21, but Nelson scored on another kickoff return making it 42-28. Alexandre scored Piedmont’s last touchdown on a 25-yard catch in the fourth quarter. PHS had 221 passing yards, with Shelby’s 62-yard strike and Lagios passing for two touchdowns, and an interception. Official stats were not provided. The Highlanders look ahead to Friday’s game against St. Mary’s at Witter Field against former PHS head coach John Trotman. The Panthers are 3-0 this season, but have played against three winless teams. “We need to come out and play our game. We have played three really good teams who have winning records and we played them all tough. Del Norte and Seaside are two strong teams who we played really tough, we just need to keep working,” said Seiden. NEXT UP Piedmont (0-3) hosts St. Mary’s on Friday, September 23 at 7:00 p.m.

articles.text: Makenna Thiel, the Post’s Athlete of the Year in 2021. and 2019 as a sophomore, is currently on the University of California tennis team in Berkeley as a second-year student. Cal is the defending Pac-12 Champion, Thiel powered through a busy summer competing at the professional level on the International Tennis Federation circuit and recently played in the Berkeley Tennis Club’s Women’s $60,000 Challenger on Monday, September 19. “For Makenna, coming out in these professional tournaments, I think she competes hard and competes well. This summer, she was able to compete a lot. We work on a lot of stuff put it into match play is the next piece,” said Cal head coach Amanda Augustus. The Berkeley Tennis Club’s Women’s Challenger often hosts several of the world’s top-100 players. For instance, Sophia Kenin won the 2018 BTC Women’s Challenger and later won the 2020 Australian Open. Thiel lost in the first round of qualifying this past weekend to No. 16 seeded Alana Smith of North Carolina State by scores of 6-2, 6-3. Smith, 22, is a graduate student and earned an honorable mention for All-ACC in 2021 and 2019, to go along with All-American doubles selections in 2021, 2020, and 2019. Smith is a tall player with a powerful serve. She recorded nine aces in Monday’s match. “This was my first hard court match in a bit over a month. It’s a big stage on center court at my former home club,” noted Thiel. “She had a really good serve and I knew I had to stay on her and focus a bit more on my service games. I think my first-serve percentage, especially in the first set, could’ve been better. I now know what I need to work on,” she added. Since Cal won the Pac-12 tennis title in April, Thiel made the second round of the W15 San Diego qualifying draw in June, made the first round main draw of another W15 tournament in San Diego later that month, made the second round of qualifying at a W15 Los Angeles tournament in July, and made the first round of the W15 Fountain Valley main draw in July., She reached the third round of W15 Lakewood in July, and was in the first round of Staff Photos Makenna Thiel, PHS Class of 2021, competed at the Berkeley Tennis Club $60,000 Women’s Challenger this week. qualifying for the W15 Frederiksberg tournament in Denmark last month. “I played a total of six pro tournaments this summer and that actually helped me get into the Berkeley Challenger with the points that I got. The atmosphere in pro level tournaments seems like it would be a lot different, but when you get there, you just stay focused and do your own thing. There are a lot more matches at the pro-level, but you see a lot of familiar faces from juniors, so it’s the same in a way,” said Thiel, Coach Augustus had high praise of Thiel and is eager to watch her development after a full year on the California roster. “She’s got about a week until our first college tournament of the season at our home courts. I’m just looking forward to seeing Makenna make the jump this year. Playing at the collegiate level is an adjustment. I think she knows what’s coming. I think she’ll be prepared for her opportunities. The fall is really great because they play at the same tournaments and everyone has an opportunity to earn spots in the lineup. I think that’s her big goal this fall,” said Augustus. California’s season starts with its Fall Invitational on September 30. The season stretches through the Fall, Winter, and concludes in late April at the Pac-12 Championship. “The training has been really good, We’ve been working a lot on our fitness,” said Thiel. “I definitely feel a lot stronger and my teammates are excellent hitting partners, I get good practice every single day. I definitely feel like I’ve improved.” Makenna Thiel is entering her sophomore year at season at the University of California.

articles.text: The Mosquito Fire roaring through Tahoe and El Dorado National Forests is now up to 76,290 acres since last week, but containment has increased to 47 percent after being at 25 percent at this time last week. It has destroyed 78 structures At 76,290 acres, it is the largest wildfire in California this year. “This increase in containment can be attributed to the hard work of firefighters who have been working around the clock to strengthen and secure containment lines in and around the communities,” wrote Cal Fire. Recent rainfall has helped efforts, allowing firefighters to create a perimeter in recent days. However, officials are expecting dry conditions to return by the end of this week. “Widespread, abundant rain over the fire area continues to reduce fire behavior, but warm, dry weather will return at the end of the week. Fire activity has slowed down, but the firefighters have not. While the rain presents a different set of challenges to the fire-suppression effort, crews continue to work, taking advantage of the lull in fire activity to secure the fire perimeter and increase containment before warm, dry weather returns,” wrote Inciweb, an official government database for wildfires. Cal Fire announced that the Photo courtesy of 2News.com Firefighting efforts have helped contain the Mosquito Fire at 47 percent as of Tuesday night. rain could provide some added complications, including potential flash floods due to the loose gravel created by the recent fires. “Thus far, the total accumulation for this storm has ranged from 1 to 2.25 inches of rain over the fire. Isolated thunderstorms moved from south to north across the fire area this afternoon. A Flash Flood Watch remains in effect for the fire area until midnight for potential ash and debris flows due to the presence of these thunderstorms,” said Cal Fire. Inciweb points out that the fire is primarily burning brush and dry timber, with large logs and duff under thick vegetation continuing smoldering conditions, which they consider to be “minimal” risk. “The fire is burning primarily in brush, and timber. The record-dry vegetation has responded to recent days and nights of high relative humidity and precipitation. However, very dry large logs and trees and the vegetation and duff under thick tree canopies all continues to smolder. Fire behavior Tuesday was minimal, consisting primarily of smoldering. From 0.75 to 2 inches of rain soaked all areas of the fire, greatly diminishing fire behavior,” said Inciweb. Inciweb adds that the current outlook for the near future includes constructing direct and indirect fire lines as conditions allow, to improve existing containment lines, and to assess needs for suppression repair. Although rain in the area is expected to subside by Wednesday, the 24-hour outlook is that fire growth will continue to be “minimal.” “Showers will begin to taper off Wednesday. A transition to a warmer, drier period will gradually start to build. Fire growth will be minimal,” per Inciweb.
articles.title: FIRE SEASON Mosquito Fire now 76,290 acres with 47 percent containment

articles.text: Photos by Cory Weaver Baritone Gerald Finley in the world premiere of John Adams’ Antony and Cleopatra at San Francisco Opera. widely cited as the leading American composer alive today. World Premiere The world premiere of John Adams’ Antony and Cleopatra opened September 10 at the War Memorial Opera House, celebrating San Francisco Opera’s 100th year. The opera is in English with supertitles; nine scenes, two acts, just over three hours. Repeat performances continue to October 5. For info: (415) 864-3330, or go online: www.artsSF.com. Berkeley composer John Adams has made a welcome attempt to bring under control the unwieldy “Antony and Cleopatra” story out of Shakespeare. Evolving from there, past composer Samuel Barber’s grand 1966 Met failure, to Adams’ world premiere, it has been boiled down from some 40 scenes and two dozen solo voices (ouch!) to Adams’ sleek, late-model version in three hours, two acts. It debuted September 10 to mark the 100th year of the San Francisco Opera. If you were waiting for gooey Pucciniesque scenes of the two lovers, this was not your opera. Instead of affairs, Adams focused on affairs of state, plus ensuing conflicts, in a historian’s more formal way. This Antony and Cleopatra is a chess match turned civil war between the ancient Romans Caesar (Augustus) and Antony, with the alluring queen Cleopatra running all over the chess board and resetting all the clocks with impunity. The punchy, highly rhythmic score festooned with electric outbursts of brass and percussion was all Adams, making no concession to popular expectations (nor any semblance of the silver screen’s Elizabeth Taylor and Richard Burton pairing). His music is at its best conveying scenes of high tension, which the opera provides in abundance. If there was more than the normal quota of opera-house dissonance, how else to portray the would-be hero sonically walking away from two wives, moving in with a minority woman from North Africa, and taking up arms in a power struggle? Historical severity was there on all counts. And Eun Sun Kim’s orchestra was aboard to make it all happen. Antony hops in and out of so many bedrooms and marriages, with yet more disasters in real combat, you wonder how ancient Rome ever survived anything. Well, civil wars are as good a way as any to start or to bring down the greatest dynasties (here, pitched battles leading to the victorious Caesar becoming the first emperor of the Roman Empire). The cast turned out much better than expected, given the cancelation of the original Cleopatra, Julia Bullock, due to pregnancy. Lyric soprano Amina Edris stepped in smartly with a sterling high range and the look of an Egyptian queen – at least, as close as you might get with this 1930s setting of 2,000-year-old history. We could certainly have done well without those 1930s perms, or films of early Ford touring cars, right, Caesar? In the early going, the Antony of baritone Gerald Finley was the night’s apex, getting strong support from tenor Paul Appleby (Caesar) as the opponent, an emperor outfitted in plain modern business suit that deserved at least a few epaulets. Stage Director Elkhanah Pulitzer and the various designers made it work with minimal tools like sliding panels and a couch or bed, all allowing for rapid scene changes. Working with a dramaturg but no credited librettist, Adams leaned on cherry-picking scenes and texts out of Shakespeare, plus adding snippets from Plutarch and Virgil. A complete overview will appear subsequently, as I could not remain to the final curtain. Earlier on, the visual highlight was playing out Antony’s disastrous naval battle at Actium, bolstered by the ballast of the robust chorus on stage – a much-needed glimpse of large-scale operadrama in a work with scarcely any show-piece soliloquies or ensembles. Acoustical Tip If you are attending, the best sonics in the whole Opera House (and lowest prices) are in the nose-bleed section of the top balcony, in Row L. An acoustic-horn effect up there magnifies the sound breathtakingly while enabling patrons to hear the pit orchestra in all its glory. Cognoscenti head up there, dressing lightly, sometimes taking binoculars. About John Adams Previous operas by Berkeleyite Adams, 75, involving historical figures and events, included Nixon in China, The Death of Klinghoffer, Dr. Atomic and The Girls of the Golden West. He is Lyric soprano Amina Edris sings the lead role as Cleopatra in John Adams’ new opera, Antony and Cleopatra.

articles.text: Due to popularity Circus Bella has added six more free showings of its newest show, Flip Flop Fly, from October 15-23. This series of performances, featuring some of the dazzling circus talent from the Bay Area, will delight audiences of all ages in a family event for all ages. Flip Flop Fly is directed by Circus Bella co-founder and director Abigail Munn. The performances will celebrate the circus’s 13th year. The 60-minute show is circus arts at its most exuberant, exploring human curiosity and sky-high imagination. Circus Bella is a diverse and talented troupe of acrobats, aerialists, jugglers, and clowns - performing to the live music of Rob Reich and the six piece Circus Bella All-Star Band. Guests are invited to bring picnic blankets and small folding chairs to all locations. A preshow performance by the Stars of Prescott Circus Theatre will also be held. To learn more visit: Circusbella.org/flipflopfly or call 415- 480-4239.
