articles.text: Berkeley Repertory Theatre is in its final week of performing Goddess from the critically-acclaimed team that created New York’s Shakespeare in the Park’s production of Merry Wise. Performances continue through September 25. Goddess is inspired by the myth of Marimba, the goddess of music, and an ancient folktale passed down by many generations across the continent of Africa. According to the folktale, Marimba created the first instruments and was the first to use her voice in song. She is also described as the most beautiful woman who ever existed and an advocate for peace, she refashioned weapons into instruments and opposed the violence of war. The play was conceived by Saheem Ali, based on book by Jocelyn Bioh. Music and Lyrics are by Michael Thurber, with choreography by Darrell Grand Moultrie. The cast includes Awa Sal Secka, Aaron Patterson, Isio-Maya Nuwere, Grasan Kingsberry, Rodrick Covington, Melessie Clark, Wade Watson and Zachary Downer. To purchase tickets, visit https://www.berkeleyrep.org/ shows/goddess/. Cast members of Berkeley Rep’s production of Goddess. Photo by Calvin Ngu
articles.title: Final week for Berkeley Rep’s Goddess

articles.text: It’s hard to imagine a more charming town than Half Moon Bay. The citizens made the decision to preserve their history… and they were successful. In some ways, time seems to stand still in Half Moon Bay. The town is like a large chunk of amber – preserved as it once was. When you go there, you are immediately in a different world. If you take Highway 92 to the end, you arrive in the camping area at the beach where there are lots of convenient facilities. It is hard to find a reasonably priced hotel room, but I did. Some of the places are luxurious in the extreme. The main street is not long, but that’s where most of the shops are. We started our eating adventure at the Flying Fish Inn. I had eaten there before and enjoyed it. The Flying Fish Inn can boast that it has the sixth best fish and chips in the entire United States. When I was a youngster, I went to the Redondo Beach pier and had fish and chips with a cornmeal batter. The Flying Fish Inn makes it the usual English way. Our large plate of fish was tender and flavorful, the French fries were blistered to a light crispness, and the tangy thousand Island dressing was fantastic. We also got the pan-seared striped bass which was also good. Breakfast places abound, and you can just walk down the street and select any one. All feature excellent breakfast pastries. The coffee was unimpressive, but the breakfast portions are big. For lunch we drove north to Sam’s famous Chowder House. The place was crowded, but we had no problem finding seats at the bar. Peter, the bartender, greeted us in a friendly manner and we ordered the famous clam chowder. It was good, but I thought it lacked a real clam flavor. The variety of restaurants in half Moon Bay is impressive. There is a restaurant for every taste, including Himalayan. Trattoria e Mare is an upscale Italian-themed restaurant. Everything here is plated beautifully and served elegantly. We began with a roasted beet and strawberry salad. Then we had a good, old Italian standby… a pan-roasted whole Bronzino fish. The roasted potatoes came with a spicy aoli. I felt that the potatoes would be improved with a few shavings of rock salt. Everywhere you go service is gracious and sincere. The servers are very accommodating, and when I told them that it was my birthday, they brought out a beautiful dessert with the words “Happy Birthday” emblazoned on the plate. Music is important in the lives of the Half Moon Bay citizens. They have lively jazz clubs, and they have resumed a concert series in the beautiful library. They also know that an orchestra legitimizes a city. Did you know that Half Moon Bay has a fine symphony orchestra – the Coastside Symphony. I remember hearing them play a concert a few years ago, and I was impressed by their enthusiasm. It is things like this that make music truly inspiring. Enjoying dinner at the Flying Fish Inn in Half Moon Bay.
articles.title: Half Moon Bay – the whole story

articles.text: In an “only in Berkeley” situation playing out at Berkeley Rep, unpaid ushers have staged two protests and have threatened to unionize over working conditions and management’s refusal to engage in any dialogue. The ushers – many of whom have been donating their time for years – are an important part of the Rep’s infrastructure. They arrive hours before each performance, check tickets, show people to their seats, answer questions, clean up after the show, and – in the past – distributed and collected programs. In exchange, they get to see the show for free. If there are seats available, the ushers can sit down during the performance; otherwise, they must watch the show on monitors in the lobby. Things were going smoothly before COVID hit. For an 8PM curtain, ushers would arrive at 6:30, have their usual ten-minute briefing, and then would have until 7:00 to eat their dinner and/or buy food from the concession stand at a discount. At 7:00 the doors to the lobby would open, and patrons could come inside. At 7:30 the theatre doors would open, and people could start taking their seats. COVID, of course, brought things to a screeching halt. When plays resumed and ushers returned, two changes were implemented: Ushers (and patrons) were no longer able to eat or drink anything in the lobby, and the concession discount inexplicably disappeared. Although understandable, the former forced ushers to go outside to eat or drink, regardless of the weather. Recently, two more policy changes were announced that pushed things to the brink. First, ushers were given less flexibility in scheduling, so that if they did not usher at least once at every play, they would be dropped. Second, and more importantly, ushers were now required to show up half an hour earlier. As a result, ushers would have 50 minutes of dead time after the evening briefing before people were even allowed into the lobby. Not surprisingly, the ushers were not happy, and asked the Front of Houses (“FOHs”, the paid employees who oversee the theatre operations at each performance) about the rationale. The FOHs told them that they agreed it was not necessary, but that it was “above their pay grade” and that they could not do anything about it. A few ushers then emailed the Front of House Director, who oversees the FOHs and who instituted the policy. She replied that Berkeley Rep was “evolving” and that if ushers couldn’t meet the time commitment, they were free to drop out. When ushers continued to email her for more explanation, she responded, “This is the last time that I will address this. Volunteering is a choice. You make the choice to come here. If you choose to come here we have rules and protocols. It’s your choice.” Ushers were understandably unhappy with both the tone and content of the FOH Director’s email and responded with their own missives. The following are quotes from emails sent by ushers obtained by this reporter: • I feel disrespected by this approach. • This situation does not demonstrate that I and my peers are valued or that our concerns about a 33% increase in preshow call time are receiving appropriate attention. • The fact that there is this much discontent should be a sign that perhaps something needs to be addressed from the management side. • Making us come earlier to hang out can be seen as not respecting our time. • We are not petulant children. Finally, things reached a breaking point. On a recent weekend, ushers showed up on time on both Saturday night and Sunday night but refused to enter the lobby for the briefing. They told the FOH that “they were protesting the start time”, “they were rebelling”, and “they were going to unionize”. Berkeley Rep is a 501(c)(3) nonprofit, which means it pays no income tax (with a few possible exceptions). Unfortunately for the ushers, it means that they cannot unionize, since California courts have ruled that volunteers for nonprofits are not employees. But it also means that its Tax Returns (excluding donor information, which is confidential) are publicly available. To its credit, Berkeley Rep provides a direct link on its website that takes you to the Federal 990, the nonprofit version of a tax return (https://www.berkeleyrep.org/media/ktpjyzem/ fy2021-990publicdisclosure.pdf). It lost well over $3 million in the year ending August 31, 2000, but then made $1.7 million in the next 12 months as donations and grants soared to offset dramatically reduced ticket sales. However, it doesn’t seem to have a problem paying salaries. According to its most recent filing, both the Artistic Director and the Managing Director earned over $280,000, and the nine highest paid salaries (including the outgoing Artistic Director) totaled $1.8 million. Not too shabby. Part of the reason that they can show such a profit and pay such salaries is because of the unpaid ushers. Using an average of ten ushers per show per night working a minimum of 4¾ hours at Berkeley’s minimum wage of $16.99 per hour, and assuming normal payroll taxes and benefits, it appears that having unpaid ushers reduces expenses by about $1,000 per performance. Since Berkeley Rep puts on over 250 performance each season, using unpaid ushers saves around a quarter of a million dollars per year (less any revenue from ushers’ purchasing tickets to any shows they might want to see). At present the situation seems to have devolved into a stalemate between an autocratic FOH Director and a group of dedicated volunteers. There is no indication that management has any idea of what is unfolding, so don’t expect any changes in the short term. However, don’t leave your seats as this Berkeleyesque drama unfolds. The Post will be there when the curtain rises on the next act, ready to keep you informed of any developments. Wiley Hoag is the Consumer Affairs reporter for the Piedmont Post.
articles.title: Berkeley Rep ushers, unpaid, stage protests

articles.text: The Asian Art Museum in San Francisco is currently exhibiting Filipino artist Carlos Villa’s work. His work will be on view through October 24. San Francisco-born Villa was a groundbreaking, 20th century modern artist whose work explores the meaning of cultural diversity in America. The exhibition, entitled Carlos Villa: Worlds in Collision, focuses mainly on the artist’s drawings, mixed-media painting, and constructions from the 1970s up until his death in 2013. Villa experimented with techniques of Western painting with materials found in non-Western art; the juxtaposition is most notably in the 1970s. The exhibition is a joint effort by the Asian Art Museum and San Francisco Art Institute (SFAI). Visit https://exhibitions. asianart.org/exhibitions/carlos-villa-worlds-in-collision/ to learn more.
articles.title: Asian Art Museum featuring exbibit by Carlos Villa

To purchase tickets, visit https://www.berkeleyrep.org/ shows/goddess/. Half Moon Bay – the whole story By Joseph Gold It’s hard to imagine a more charming town than Half Moon Bay. The citizens made the decision to preserve their history… and they were successful. In some ways, time seems to stand still in Half Moon Bay. The town is like a large chunk of amber – preserved as it once was. When you go there, you are immediately in a different world. If you take Highway 92 to the end, you arrive in the camping area at the beach where there are lots of convenient facilities. It is hard to find a reasonably priced hotel room, but I did. Some of the places are luxurious in the extreme. The main street is not long, but that’s where most of the shops are. We started our eating adventure at the Flying Fish Inn. I had eaten there before and enjoyed it. The Flying Fish Inn can boast that it has the sixth best fish and chips in the entire United States. When I was a youngster, I went to the Redondo Beach pier and had fish and chips with a cornmeal batter. The Flying Fish Inn makes it the usual English way. Our large plate of fish was tender and flavorful, the French fries were blistered to a light crispness, and the tangy thousand Island dressing was fantastic. We also got the pan-seared striped bass which was also good. Breakfast places abound, and you can just walk down the street and select any one. All feature excellent breakfast pastries. The coffee was unimpressive, but the breakfast portions are big. For lunch we drove north to Sam’s famous Chowder House. The place was crowded, but we had no problem finding seats at the bar. Peter, the bartender, greeted us in a friendly manner and we ordered the famous clam chowder. It was good, but I thought it lacked a real clam flavor. The variety of restaurants in half Moon Bay is impressive. There is a restaurant for every taste, including Himalayan. Trattoria e Mare is an upscale Italian-themed restaurant. Everything here is plated beautifully and served elegantly. We began with a roasted beet and strawberry salad. Then we had a good, old Italian standby… a pan-roasted whole Bronzino fish. The roasted potatoes came with a spicy aoli. I felt that the potatoes would be improved with a few shavings of rock salt. Everywhere you go service is gracious and sincere. The servers are very accommodating, and when I told them that it was my birthday, they brought out a beautiful dessert with the words “Happy Birthday” emblazoned on the plate. Music is important in the lives of the Half Moon Bay citizens. They have lively jazz clubs, and they have resumed a concert series in the beautiful library. They also know that an orchestra legitimizes a city. Did you know that Half Moon Bay has a fine symphony orchestra – the Coastside Symphony. I remember hearing them play a concert a few years ago, and I was impressed by their enthusiasm. It is things like this that make music truly inspiring. Asian Art Museum featuring exbibit by Carlos Villa The Asian Art Museum in San Francisco is currently exhibiting Filipino artist Carlos Villa’s work. His work will be on view through October 24. San Francisco-born Villa was a groundbreaking, 20th century modern artist whose work explores the meaning of cultural diversity in America. The exhibition, entitled Carlos Villa: Worlds in Collision, focuses mainly on the artist’s drawings, mixed-media painting, and constructions from the 1970s up until his death in 2013. Villa experimented with techniques of Western painting with materials found in non-Western art; the juxtaposition is most notably in the 1970s. The exhibition is a joint effort by the Asian Art Museum and San Francisco Art Institute (SFAI). Visit https://exhibitions. asianart.org/exhibitions/carlos-villa-worlds-in-collision/ to learn more. Berkeley Rep ushers, unpaid, stage protests By Wiley Hoag In an “only in Berkeley” situation playing out at Berkeley Rep, unpaid ushers have staged two protests and have threatened to unionize over working conditions and management’s refusal to engage in any dialogue. The ushers – many of whom have been donating their time for years – are an important part of the Rep’s infrastructure. They arrive hours before each performance, check tickets, show people to their seats, answer questions, clean up after the show, and – in the past – distributed and collected programs. In exchange, they get to see the show for free. If there are seats available, the ushers can sit down during the performance; otherwise, they must watch the show on monitors in the lobby. Things were going smoothly before COVID hit. For an 8PM curtain, ushers would arrive at 6:30, have their usual ten-minute briefing, and then would have until 7:00 to eat their dinner and/or buy food from the concession stand at a discount. At 7:00 the doors to the lobby would open, and patrons could come inside. At 7:30 the theatre doors would open, and people could start taking their seats. COVID, of course, brought things to a screeching halt. When plays resumed and ushers returned, two changes were implemented: Ushers (and patrons) were no longer able to eat or drink anything in the lobby, and the concession discount inexplicably disappeared. Although understandable, the former forced ushers to go outside to eat or drink, regardless of the weather. Recently, two more policy changes were announced that pushed things to the brink. First, ushers were given less flexibility in scheduling, so that if they did not usher at least once at every play, they would be dropped. Second, and more importantly, ushers were now required to show up half an hour earlier. As a result, ushers would have 50 minutes of dead time after the evening briefing before people were even allowed into the lobby. Not surprisingly, the ushers were not happy, and asked the Front of Houses (“FOHs”, the paid employees who oversee the theatre operations at each performance) about the rationale. The FOHs told them that they agreed it was not necessary, but that it was “above their pay grade” and that they could not do anything about it. A few ushers then emailed the Front of House Director, who oversees the FOHs and who instituted the policy. She replied that Berkeley Rep was “evolving” and that if ushers couldn’t meet the time commitment, they were free to drop out. When ushers continued to email her for more explanation, she responded, “This is the last time that I will address this. Volunteering is a choice. You make the choice to come here. If you choose to come here we have rules and protocols. It’s your choice.” Ushers were understandably unhappy with both the tone and content of the FOH Director’s email and responded with their own missives. The following are quotes from emails sent by ushers obtained by this reporter: • I feel disrespected by this approach. • This situation does not demonstrate that I and my peers are valued or that our concerns about a 33% increase in preshow call time are receiving appropriate attention. • The fact that there is this much discontent should be a sign that perhaps something needs to be addressed from the management side. • Making us come earlier to hang out can be seen as not respecting our time. • We are not petulant children. Finally, things reached a breaking point. On a recent weekend, ushers showed up on time on both Saturday night and Sunday night but refused to enter the lobby for the briefing. They told the FOH that “they were protesting the start time”, “they were rebelling”, and “they were going to unionize”. Berkeley Rep is a 501(c)(3) nonprofit, which means it pays no income tax (with a few possible exceptions). Unfortunately for the ushers, it means that they cannot unionize, since California courts have ruled that volunteers for nonprofits are not employees. But it also means that its Tax Returns (excluding donor information, which is confidential) are publicly available. To its credit, Berkeley Rep provides a direct link on its website that takes you to the Federal 990, the nonprofit version of a tax return (https://www.berkeleyrep.org/media/ktpjyzem/ fy2021-990publicdisclosure.pdf). It lost well over $3 million in the year ending August 31, 2000, but then made $1.7 million in the next 12 months as donations and grants soared to offset dramatically reduced ticket sales. However, it doesn’t seem to have a problem paying salaries. According to its most recent filing, both the Artistic Director and the Managing Director earned over $280,000, and the nine highest paid salaries (including the outgoing Artistic Director) totaled $1.8 million. Not too shabby. Part of the reason that they can show such a profit and pay such salaries is because of the unpaid ushers. Using an average of ten ushers per show per night working a minimum of 4¾ hours at Berkeley’s minimum wage of $16.99 per hour, and assuming normal payroll taxes and benefits, it appears that having unpaid ushers reduces expenses by about $1,000 per performance. Since Berkeley Rep puts on over 250 performance each season, using unpaid ushers saves around a quarter of a million dollars per year (less any revenue from ushers’ purchasing tickets to any shows they might want to see). At present the situation seems to have devolved into a stalemate between an autocratic FOH Director and a group of dedicated volunteers. There is no indication that management has any idea of what is unfolding, so don’t expect any changes in the short term. However, don’t leave your seats as this Berkeleyesque drama unfolds. The Post will be there when the curtain rises on the next act, ready to keep you informed of any developments. Wiley Hoag is the Consumer Affairs reporter for the Piedmont Post.

articles.text: A joint art show will be on view at the Piedmont Center for the Arts from October 1-9. Ellen Dreibelbis, a figurative artist, and John Q. McDonald a landscape painter, will have an exhibit titled Something About the Light. Gallery hours are 11 a.m. to 2 p.m. on Saturday and Sunday, October 1-2 and October 8-9. Dreibelbis of Oakland creates figurative paintings that illuminate and celebrate the beauty and wisdom of the world’s people. She is often deeply moved by the way the light illuminates an object, bringing forth its power and mystery. From that evocative beginning comes a journey full of risk, uncertainty and restatement, through which she strives to build the aesthetic architecture combining composition, value, color, and edges which anchor the more intangible qualities that emerge in the process of painting. As each painting seems to have its own voice, she has learned to be still and listen to it rather than imposing her own ideas, and never knows how a painting will turn out until all parts ring true. McDonald of Pleasanton uses light to enhance the graphical drama of landscapes in California and beyond. Inspired in part by modern landscape painters such as Robert Bechtle, Gerhard Richter, Georgia O’Keefe and Edward Hopper, his work tends to focus on the interaction between memory, the human-made and the natural in our landscape. An astronomer by trade and therefore used to relying upon light, he endeavors to capture in his painting the unique quality of light found in the different places he has visited and inhabited, particularly the bright light of California and the West. He seeks to express the manner in which the things we create, the places we build, establish their meaning and presence in our environment. Friends for years, this is their first joint art show. Warming Hut SF by John Q. McDonald, Oil on Canvas, 16” x 12” Peruvian Boy, by Ellen Dreibelbis, pastel on archival paper, 18” x 14”

articles.text: Come enjoy a wide range of music, art and special events throughout the year. Saturday, October 1, 11:00 a.m. Exhibition by 2 local artists This opening begins two weekends showing the work of two local artists in a most timely show they have entitled “Something about the Light…” comprised of figurative paintings that celebrate the beauty and wisdom of the peoples of the world by Ellen Dreibelbis, along with paintings enhancing graphical drama in landscapes by John Q. McDonald, exploring the relationships between human structures and their natural surroundings. Entry to the show is free. Food tickets are $10 at the door, and a souvenir beer glass for $15 will admit you to unlimited tastes of the various brews. Seating will be limited to the first 70 attendees. Take part in a Live Auction and FundA-Need to benefit Left Coast’s programs. Tickets for the Gala are $150 per person. For details, see www.leftcoastensemble.org/gala-2022. The Chamber Music Society of San Francisco opens its 10th anniversary season with a return to Ludwig van Beethoven’s Opus 132, String Quartet in A minor, the masterpiece that brought these fine musicians together a decade ago. In this and other late works, Beethoven turned inward, leaving us with some of his most exquisite and transcendental music. The program will also include Mozart’s Dissonance String Quartet in C Major, and Caroline Shaw’s Valencia. Get your advance tickets now at https://bit.ly/3TpKMUZ for this 90-minute concert, which was postponed from September 17.

articles.text: In the Heights plays until October 16 Berkeley Playhouse is currently performing Lin Manuel Miranda’s musical, In the Heights. Directed by Melissa Martinez, it will be at Berkeley Playhouse through October 16, In the Heights is the second musical theater production developed by Miranda. His first production, Hamilton, told the story of Alexander Hamilton and federalism with a modern tune. This production draws on similar musical themes but tells the story of growing up in the Washington Heights neighborhood of New York City. The Berkeley Playhouse offers a season pass for avid theater fans or single show passes. The theater is located at 2640 College Avenue in Berkeley. For tickets or season passes visit https://tickets.berkeleyplayhouse.org or call the box office at (510) 845-8542 x351. Tickets purchased at the door are cash only. Cristina Hernandez (Nina Rosario) and Jordan Covington (Benny) embrace in the romantic climax of the show.

articles.text: Daisy Edgar-Jones’s Kya stars in Where the Crawdads Sing. Where the Crawdads Sing is a Southern gothic story based on the 2018 best-selling novel by Della Owens. As of this writing, it has sold more than 12 million copies worldwide and has developed a passionate fan base. It was inevitable that it would find its way to the screen. Set in the small North Carolina town of Barley Cove, the story spans some 20 years, from the 1950s to the 1970s. The film, which doesn’t quite follow the narrative plot of the book, opens with a young woman, Kya Clark (Daisy Edgar-Jones), also called “the Marsh Girl,” on trial for murder. She is charged with killing Chase Andrews (Taylor John-Smith), a popular young man from a wealthy and prominent family. Her defense counsel is a retired attorney, Tom Milton (David Strathairn), who has known Kya since she was a child and is committed to her innocence. The tale is told in a series of flashbacks, beginning with Kya as a young girl living on the edge of a stretching marsh with her mother, siblings, and abusive, drunken father. Her mother one day simply walks away, soon to be followed by her brother and sisters. Kya finds herself left with her father. But before long he vanishes as well. Barely a tween, she finds herself alone, living in the shack, struggling to survive, while relying on her knowledge of the marsh, her innate intelligence, and resourcefulness. And so, Kya develops into a fiercely independent young woman who wanders the marsh in her father’s old boat and sells mussels to a local store owner in exchange for needed supplies. She did go to school – for one day – but was laughed at by the children when she stood before them barefooted and uncombed. Years later she is taught to read by a local boy, Tate Walker (Taylor John-Smith), who has known Kya since they were children (they are now in their teens). Once she discovers books, a new and astonishing world opens up to her, and she begins to read about the marsh animals. She soon sketches them in her notebooks, demonstrating an extraordinary descriptive talent. Where the Crawdads Sing gradually develops into two love stories involving Tate and Chase (it’s Chase that Kya is accused of killing). But the essence of the film is the solitude of the marsh and the small shack where Kya has lived alone, shunned by the judgmental townspeople. Time and place, as well as the splendor of the marsh, become as central to this story as are its characters. Those who loved the book will embrace the film. Others may find it less intense than it might have been, especially the trial. But as a whole, it is engaging and at times irresistible. Where the Crawdads Sing. Directed by Olivia Newman. Starring Daisy Edgar-Jones, Taylor John-Smith, Harris Dickinson. 2 hrs., 5 min. PG-13. Appearing in theaters and streaming on Prime/ VUDU.

articles.text: Review by Chris Honoré Pedro Almodovar has won two Oscars, six BAFTAs (British), nine Goyas (Spanish), honorary doctorates from Harvard and Oxford, and has been working for 40 years at the craft of filmmaking. His chosen medium has allowed him to repeatedly examine the kaleidoscopic richness of the human condition. In his most recent film, Pain and Glory, he has created a spare narrative, never stark, never confused by vanity, but one that is close-to-the-bone subtle and nuanced, offered written and directed by Almodovar, who is now in his 70s. The lead character, Salvador Mallo, is a world-famous writer and filmmaker named Salvador Mallo, superbly portrayed by Antonio Banderas who is a ringer for Almodovar, down to the clothes he wears, his graying beard and spiky hair. The setting, almost exclusively, is Mallo’s Madrid apartment (recreated from Almodovar’s own apartment, with his personal art one the walls). Mallo is a man who is aging badly and feels betrayed by his body. And to be clear about the vagaries of that betrayal, at the outset of the film, using animation, Mallo, in voice over, lists the afflictions that plague him: sciatica, depression, tinnitus, migraines, insomnia, a fused back, a throat that abruptly closes causing uncontrollable coughing, all buffered by alcohol and meds. Professionally he refuses to write because physically he cannot direct what he might create. He wonders if he will ever work again, a voiced lament to a longago collaborator, actor Alberto Crespo (Asier Etxeandia), a man he has not seen for some 30 years, and with whom he smokes heroin for the first time – anything to relieve the pain. When he falls into a heroin-induced reverie and dreams about his childhood and his mother, Jacinta (Penelope Cruz). He remembers an apartment-like cave they lived in when the family left their village. He remembers this underground home being filled with his mother’s love. In truth, Pain and Glory is a kind of reverie, often dream-like, when Mallo, lives hermit-like and is visited or rescued by loyal women who satellite his life while caring for him. In is a series of revelations, often steeped in regret, his story now a soft lament. But the audience must keep in mind that this film is told by an unreliable narrator (Mallo/ Almodovar) and is framed by a spectrum of startling primary colors that belie Mallo’s condition and viewpoint. Deep reds enter almost every scene, often coordinated with his shirts and the window coverings; rainbows of colors are everywhere, in his flashbacks and in his daily life, a seeming contradiction. In an unexpected way, the exposition is uplifting, for Mallo still refuses to yield. He even writes as if that very act is one of self-deception, yet the words are his own. Pain and Glory is a quiet meditation on aging and the physical betrayal that accompanies that experience. For Mallo, his physical pain is a reminder of a reality from which he can find no exit. He acknowledges that he is in the autumn of his life, heading toward winter. His dreams – his mother, of her washing clothes by a river, singing with the other village women – are of spring. And even now his thoughts sway like long stalks of grass, bending back and forth, only slowing righting themselves. This is his life, wistfully told, tenderly offered, a nexus of pain and glory while he hopes that still there is work ahead. A fact that is demonstrated so eloquently in this film. Pain and Glory. Written and directed by Pedro Almodovar. In Spanish with subtitles. Starring Antonio Banderas, Penelope Cruz and Asier Etxeandia. 1 hr., 52 min. Rated R. Released in 2019. Now streaming on VUDU/Prime.
articles.title: Pain and Glory a beautiful film and story told by a master

Now streaming on VUDU/Prime. 4020 Piedmont Avenue Oakland, CA 94611 Hours: Tuesday-Saturday 11am-5:30pm Sunday 1pm-5pm Benefitting Piedmont Education for 40 Years! dressbestforless.org MOVIES FOR KIDS Where the Crawdads Sing a lovely story Daisy Edgar-Jones’s Kya stars in Where the Crawdads Sing. By Chris Honoré Where the Crawdads Sing is a Southern gothic story based on the 2018 best-selling novel by Della Owens. As of this writing, it has sold more than 12 million copies worldwide and has developed a passionate fan base. It was inevitable that it would find its way to the screen. Set in the small North Carolina town of Barley Cove, the story spans some 20 years, from the 1950s to the 1970s. The film, which doesn’t quite follow the narrative plot of the book, opens with a young woman, Kya Clark (Daisy Edgar-Jones), also called “the Marsh Girl,” on trial for murder. She is charged with killing Chase Andrews (Taylor John-Smith), a popular young man from a wealthy and prominent family. Her defense counsel is a retired attorney, Tom Milton (David Strathairn), who has known Kya since she was a child and is committed to her innocence. The tale is told in a series of flashbacks, beginning with Kya as a young girl living on the edge of a stretching marsh with her mother, siblings, and abusive, drunken father. Her mother one day simply walks away, soon to be followed by her brother and sisters. Kya finds herself left with her father. But before long he vanishes as well. Barely a tween, she finds herself alone, living in the shack, struggling to survive, while relying on her knowledge of the marsh, her innate intelligence, and resourcefulness. And so, Kya develops into a fiercely independent young woman who wanders the marsh in her father’s old boat and sells mussels to a local store owner in exchange for needed supplies. She did go to school – for one day – but was laughed at by the children when she stood before them barefooted and uncombed. Years later she is taught to read by a local boy, Tate Walker (Taylor John-Smith), who has known Kya since they were children (they are now in their teens). Once she discovers books, a new and astonishing world opens up to her, and she begins to read about the marsh animals. She soon sketches them in her notebooks, demonstrating an extraordinary descriptive talent. Where the Crawdads Sing gradually develops into two love stories involving Tate and Chase (it’s Chase that Kya is accused of killing). But the essence of the film is the solitude of the marsh and the small shack where Kya has lived alone, shunned by the judgmental townspeople. Time and place, as well as the splendor of the marsh, become as central to this story as are its characters. Those who loved the book will embrace the film. Others may find it less intense than it might have been, especially the trial. But as a whole, it is engaging and at times irresistible. Where the Crawdads Sing. Directed by Olivia Newman. Starring Daisy Edgar-Jones, Taylor John-Smith, Harris Dickinson. 2 hrs., 5 min. PG-13. Appearing in theaters and streaming on Prime/ VUDU.

pages.text: 22 Wednesday, September 21, 2022 Features The Wine Corner The Wines of Georgia invent in a modern world; you could only inherit them through the mists of time, maybe as far back as human records go.” Historians note that Georgia could be seen to be the crucible from which the great majority of Europe’s wine grape varieties emerged. Winemaking evidence has been found in Georgia dating back into the sixth millennium B.C. How did they make wine? Georgians would hollow out a tree trunk, fill it with grapes, tread them, and then tip the juice, skins, pips and even stems into a big beeswax-lined clay jar called a kvevri. They would then seal it and leave the juice to ferment, for six months to a year before cracking it open and drinking it. What is amazing is that this is still the way they make wine in Georgia. For the first time in my life, I had the opportunity to sample some of the wines of Georgia and was absolutely delighted to experience these vibrant, exciting and totally new flavors. In terms of accessing these wines, K&L Wines has a small selection of Georgian wines, or you can contact Marion Helluy at mhelluy@ colangelopr.com for information on availability. Large clay urns called Kvevri are used to ferment and age the wines. articles.text: One of my favorite types of design projects is when we are able to do a remodel that completely transforms an existing house. In some situations, the transformational change can be triggered simply by a client’s desire for change and improvement to the existing house. The extent of change can be the need to move basic functions from one part of the house to another, like the kitchen, or the bathroom or laundry. articles.text: Dear Abby: I heard there was an app that translates cat meows into plain English? Is this true or is this horse poop? Do you think there’s one for dogs? Howling woof. –Tank the Lab, Hank the Cat and Momma Anne Dear Tank, Hank and Momma Anne, There are several apps that proclaim to translate cat talk into English. I am somewhat skeptical yet always optimistic. MeowTalk Translator is a mobile app that says it can decode basic cat’s meows into basic English. Apparently, cats use different types of melodies when they are trying to communicate (and I believe dogs do, too.) MeowTalk uses machine-learning algorithms to decode them. In 2021, MeowTalk researchers reported that the app could distinguish nine different meow intents with 90% accuracy. I did find others. There’s one called: Human-to Cat Translator. another titled Cat Translate: Talk to Kitty, one other My Talking Pet: Dog and Cat Translator, and one called: Dog Translator, What My Dog is Saying. The prices on these vary and some reviews advise you pay for a premium version and avoid the ads. I am not sure if any of these work. The one thing they allow you to do is to easily store your cat’s meows so that when they run out of their nine lives, you can still listen to those recordings and remember those funny days. As for dogs, there are a few interesting apps that translate and offer whistle techniques and games: Human to Dog Translator and DogSpeak look promising, and a start-up, Zoolingua, is working on an A.I. powered woof translator that analyzes canine vocalizations and even dog body language. The urge to talk to animals is centuries old and it makes sense that data can be used to help give animals another voice. But I can’t help wonder if we will always want to hear what they have to say. Woof-bah (canine for thank you). –Abby Please address all questions, concerns and fun activities about any animal to Abby at Melandogs@gmail.com. articles.text: Oakland Zoo is excited to host its annual “Healthy Living Festival,” presented by the United Seniors of Oakland and Alameda County. This year’s event will take place on Thursday, September 29, from 9:00 a.m.to 2:00 p.m. The festival promotes health and wellness for aging adults, and includes free food, music, fun and more. A free lunch will be given to all pre-registered participants. The last day to register is this Friday, September 23. “We are honored to be once again asked to host this year’s event, and we’re grateful to do our part to help ensure the health of our senior community. We are here to support all ages, both as a resource and as a long-standing destination dedicated to animals, nature, and education,” said Nik Dehejia, CEO of Oakland Zoo. The Healthy Living Festival is a free event for seniors 55+ living in Alameda County to promote health and wellness. In previous years, this annual event drew an average of more than 2,000 participants. “For many, getting vaccinated, tested, and staying social in a safe way has been a challenge. Oakland Zoo continues to be our gracious and flexible partner, and I am excited that this year’s Healthy Living Festival is a safely organized drive-through, offering all three necessities to those who need them the most”, said Alameda County Supervisor Nate Miley. As the Zoo currently celebrates its Centennial year, it will continue to expand its outreach in the community. For more information, visit: Oaklandzoo.org/programs-andevents/healthy-living-festival Oakland Mayor Libby Schaaf dances with guests at Oakland Zoo’s Healthy Living Festival last year.
articles.title: Oakland Zoo to host annual Healthy Living Festival for seniors on Sept. 29

articles.text: A strong turnout of 37 showed up for the weekly Walking on Wednesdays on September 14. An extra incentive planned was a visit to the beautiful garden of Christina Schneck on Estates Drive. Christina gave the group a tour a couple of years earlier. The group started off taking a familiar route up Highland to Sheridan and Wildwood Avenues. The group continued up Hampton Road to its intersection with St. James Drive. They went down to La Salle Avenue where two white columns mark this entrance to what was the St. James Woods development, a large real estate project about a hundred years ago. It was noted that all the sidewalks throughout the development have a four tile per section inlay pattern. This original design has been continued to this day when sidewalks are repaired. They continued on past Corpus Christi Church to Park Way and then up Estates Drive where Christina was outside waiting for the group. She shared the history of the garden she has created. It started about 35 years ago when she began the transformation of a traditional grass front yard to the impressive garden it is today. It starts with the car strip at the street curb with a quilt-like artwork of different succulents and other plants. The front yard is equally impressive, and composed of larger plants and trees, some of which are 30 years old. Christina then led the group to her backyard where more of her gardening creation was on display. Tall redwoods provide shade for her forest of plants. There is also a large urn that is a fountain in the middle of yard that attracts fantail pigeons, hummingbirds, blue jays, crows, and others. The fountain provides water and also safety for the birds. Additionally, the garden includes a number of metal sculptures by local sculptor Mark Bulwinkle, who works in cut steel. It was fun to see what Christina’s years of hard work have created. The walkers thanked Christina for her hospitality and then made their way back via Sandringham Place, Cambrian, and St. James. It was a long walk, more than 3-1/2 miles, but seeing the natural beauty that Christina has created made it well worthwhile. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation Department is required at https://tinyurl. com/3ethkehu. Wednesday Walkers on September 14 at the home of Christina Schneck. Pictured are Lisa Euphrat, Edith Lee, Alicia Rivera, Jim Kuo, Elizabeth Richter, Charlene Louie, Noemi Alvarado, Lois Price, Pat Keller, Helen and Quincy Dong, Gloria DaSilva, Sherry Jacobs, Joyce and Bill Ahern, Adrienne Hamlin, Kat Lang, Nadine Guffanti, Ann Quinby, Renee Goldhammer, Rob Smith, Melba Yee, Alan Goldhammer, Brenda Ferrero, Judy Wang, Harriette Louie, Martin Levy, Sarah Johnson, Nancy and Larry Olsen, Matt Gerhardt, Mike Gallant, Ian Morgan, Jasmine Cai, Elane Rehr, Meghan Bennett, and Dick Carter.

articles.text: October 5, 1940 – September 1, 2022 PIEDMONT, CA – Jim McCrea, 81, resident of Piedmont, formerly of Cuba City, WI, passed away peacefully in Oakland on September 1, 2022, following a nearly yearlong battle with cancer. Born October 5, 1940 in Cuba City, WI to Guerdon “Butch” and Sylvia (Lacke) McCrea. Survived by his life partner of 50 years, Gregory L. Jurin, who he married in 2015; his sister, Barbara (Ron) McDermott, of Dubuque, IA; nephews, Brad (Brittney) McDermott of Glenview, IL and their children, Lucy, Tate, and Mae; Scott (Catie) McDermott of Atlanta, GA and their children, Jack and Finn; and niece, Sara (Mark) Kasemeier of Dubuque, IA and their children, Charlie and Beau. He was preceded in death by his parents and sister Karen McCrea. Jim graduated from Cuba City High School (1958) and Marquette University, Milwaukee (1962) to enlist in the US Air Force as a Captain. Jim continued to serve in the Air Force 8 years then moved to the San Francisco Bay Area and spent the majority of his career in Human Resources within a wide variety of businesses, primarily banking, retiring in 2003. During his military and professional careers, Jim developed a love of travel, and was fortunate to travel extensively during his retirement years. He was the appointed organizer of family reunions, and he enjoyed returnJames Philip McCrea ing to Cuba City for many high school reunions. Jim was such a wonderful man of lively faith and someone passionate about social, political, and environmental justice. He died on the World Day of Prayer for the Care of Creation. Family and friends are respectfully invited to attend his Vigil Friday, September 23rd 7pm and funeral liturgy and reception 10am, Saturday September 24th both at Corpus Christi Church, 322 Saint James Drive, Piedmont, CA. For those in Wisconsin, private services October 10th in Cuba City. Internment at a later date at St. Rose Cemetery, Cuba City. Remembrances may be made in Jim’s name to the Dominican Sisters of Sinsinawa, at their Motherhouse, 585 Co Rd Z, Sinsinawa, WI 53824, or charity of your choice. Deer Creek Funeral Services (510) 317-7890

articles.text: The First Monday Reading Group met outside the Japanese Tea House in Piedmont Park on September 12 and had a lively discussion of Magpie Murders, a 2016 mystery novel by English writer Anthony Horowitz and the first novel in his Susan Ryeland series. The book has been translated into multiple languages and has been adapted into a sixpart PBS Masterpiece Theatre drama series that will be aired in the U.S. and the UK in October. The story is about the murder of a mystery author and utilizes an unusual story-within-a story format. Susan Ryeland is the editor of mystery author Alan Conway, who is known for his novels about detective Atticus Pünd, described as a difficult person. Fans are eagerly awaiting Conway’s latest novel, rumored to be the last in the series, but when Ryeland reads the manuscript she realizes it is unfinished. Soon after she hears that Conway has died. To find the book’s final chapters Susan begins her own investigation. She learns that Conway’s novel may have been based on true events, which might have led to his murder. The group’s response to the book was largely positive. Many readers enjoyed Horowitz’s creativity, especially his use of the story-within-a story and murder-within-a murder structure. There are two books here, but the author blended them together so that they support and reinforce one another. The book was praised for its interesting characters. Readers felt a connection to Susan Ryeland and her personal challenges and empathized in her quest to find the missing chapters and solve the murders of Pünd and Conway. Horowitz has a lot going on for the reader to consider. It is a mystery with many characters, and it seems everyone has a solid reason to be Conway’s killer. The reader is challenged with what turns out to be an impossible task of figuring it all out and solving the crimes before Horowitz reveals the answers. It was noted that reading novels keeps minds’ sharp, and this type of mystery with all its clues and possibilities was good mental exercise for the group. However, there was some criticism as well. This book is not written in a simple Agatha Christie who-done-it on-the-train structure. For some members of the group, the story was too complex and confusing. The book’s two stories and 560 pages were a lot to manage. There were many names and events to keep track of, and it was impossible to know what was relevant for solving the crimes. The story-within-a story structure also made the storyline difficult for some to follow. The conclusion with Conway’s killer revealed was not believable for some readers, although it was accepted that suspending some level of disbelief is required in this type of fiction. It was also agreed that mysteries like this one are usually for entertainment and “guilty pleasure,” and for most readers Magpie Murders delivered on this. Horowitz wove all the evidence together at the book’s conclusion to solve the causes of the two deaths, and also provided a somewhat happy ending for Susan Ryeland. He also did that for most readers, who almost universally are going to watch the PBS mini-series in October. Ut was noted that among those participating in the discussion was Piedmont resident Bob Hall who has written a number of Ben Franklin mysteries under his full name, Robert Lee Hall. His works include: Exit Sherlock Holmes, The Great Detectives Final Days, Murder at San Simeon, and Benjamin Franklin Takes the Case. He has been the principal theater reviewer for the Piedmont Post for more than 20 years. The readers had previously selected Joel Richard Paul’s non-fiction Unlikely Allies, the true story of how three men used espionage, betrayal, and sexual deception to help win the American Revolution, for October. After some discussion, the readers picked Klara and the Sun by Nobel laureate Kazuo Ishiguro for November. This is an intriguing novel about how artificial intelligence might play a role in our futures. The group discussed a number of non-fiction possibilities for December, but decided to hold off on a selection until their meeting on October 3, at 1:30 p.m. at the Japanese Tea House. New readers are welcome to join the group. There is no fee to participate, but registration is required by calling 510-420-3070. Participating in the First Monday Reading Group discussion on September 12 were Jerry Gragg, Carol Long, Phil Witte, Nancy Henn, Mike Henn, Peggy Rourke, Sarah Johnson, Lois Price, Adrienne Hamlin, Melba Yee, Martin Levy, Ken Young, Robert and Madeline Hall, and Dick Carter, in addition to first-time participants Dale Benveniste and Sarah Moldenhauser-Salazar.
articles.title: Monday Reading Group digs into Magpie Murders

articles.text: To experience the magic of Broadway musicals from the comfort of your own home, residents can now enroll in a class online through Piedmont Adult School titled “The Musicals of Rodgers and Hammerstein.” From familiar shows like South Pacific and The King and I, to less well-known ones like Allegro and Pipe Dream, this class will explore 11 musicals created by the famous team of Richard Rodgers and Oscar Hammerstein. The class will meet twice, on October 13 and 20, and registration is now open. The class will feature video clips of song and dance numbers from the shows and live commentary by the instructor about the background content and creative process behind their creation. Instructor Ken Ross has extensive experience in musical theater as a director, performer, teacher and long-time theater attendee. For 20 years he was head of the theater department at Las Positas Instructor Ken Ross has performed featured roles in seven musicals at Woodminster Summer Musicals and currently serves on the Woodminster Theater Advisory Board. College in Livermore, and in earlier years he was theater instructor and director of plays and musicals at Bishop O’Dowd High School and the Athenian School in Danville. To register, visit Piedmontadultschool.org or call the Adult School office at 594-2655. The Musicals of Rodgers and Hammerstein October 13, 20 (2 sessions) Thursdays, 7:00-9:00 p.m. $54 Online Instructor: Ken Ross

articles.text: Remembering James Motlow Chance meetings happen for a reason. On a cool December day last year, my sister and I with two friends had the great fortune of visiting Locke, CA. It’s not exactly a well-known town. For a reunion weekend with friends, one might have wondered why we picked the Sacramento Delta, given all the other exciting attractions in the San Francisco Bay Area. Pulling up to Locke, I had the distinct sense that I had stepped back in time. Wood frame buildings looked like they had been untouched for decades. There was a leaning theater façade, houses which sat on foundations of cinder blocks, and a gambling house museum that harkened to a way of life that I could only imagine. The town was literally made up of four streets. My sister had visited once before and was fascinated with the history of this once all-Chinese town. She had booked us a private tour and was thrilled to find that our tour guide was none other than James Motlow, a Locke resident, photographer and co-author of the book, Bitter Melon: Inside America’s Last Rural Chinese Town. It is a poignant photographic oral memoir that tells the history and legacy of Locke and its Chinese community. Readers of this article will be interested in knowing that Motlow was also a former Piedmont resident from 1992 to 2009. Spending two hours with James was like getting a rare opportunity to meet the people of Locke themselves. We learned how he befriended Jone Ho Leong, who at first was skeptical of this “outsider.” We began to understand the quiet ways of life for so many of the Chinese families who lived there. As younger generations grew up and left, few returned to Locke. James’ earnestness and his great love for the community of Locke were impossible to forget. We corresponded for months afterwards, about his dreams for a film about the history and stories of Locke, about the release of recent films covering Chinese American history – Far East, Deep South and The Six – and about plans to bring friends, colleagues, and fellow Piedmonters to visit Locke. We joined the Locke Foundation and purchased a tile for Locke Memorial Park to commemorate our weekend visit, with a special thank you note to James. Sadly, I received news that James passed away unexpectedly in August. My sister and I attended the memorial service in the gardens of Locke where nearly 150 family, friends, and colleagues gathered. Listening to their testimonials, we began to understand even more the impact of his life and work – and why he had made such an indelible impression in our one chance meeting. Friends Bitter Melon: Inside America’s Last Rural Chinese Town by James Motlow spoke of his commitment to history as well as the love and joy he infused into his art. James had seen the “magic of Locke.” Beyond the faded past and the failing buildings, he understood the deep legacy of the town – and he became part of the history of Locke. So if you are ever in the Sacramento area, make time to visit Locke. Stop by the Visitor Center and pick up a copy of Bitter Melon or one of James’ signed prints. And if you want a tour by James himself, play this video created by the University of the Pacific https://www.youtube.com/ watch?v=13ZpNaJK0jo. Step back in time and immerse yourself in a community that once was – and still is. Support the legacy of Locke and the memory of James Motlow by donating to the Locke Foundation at: http://www.locke-foundation.org Leslie Wang (left), Tina Wang, Joan Lo, and Eliza Lo Chin with author and former Piedmont resident James Motlow. articles.text: On their latest outing the Piedmont Seniors visited a quirky new museum in San Rafael on Thursday, July 21. The Museum of International Propaganda was founded seven years ago by Tom and Lilka Areton. The husband and wife team visited over 80 countries in their travels, with an eye towards collecting vintage propaganda wherever they went. Mr. Areton is from the Czechoslovak Socialist Republic where there was only one political party, the Communist party. Mr. Areton told the Piedmont group that the “only election you had was that you could vote on Friday or Saturday!” The Aretons are very careful not to include current political issues in their displays, such as Biden, or Trump. Instead, their focus is on the political propaganda of the 20th century, which includes propaganda from Italy, North Korea, Iran. Nazi Germany, China, and Cuba, along with a myriad of books from the private collection of the Aretons. Prior to Covid, they hosted weekly movie screenings dedicated to different aspects of propaganda, complete with wine from their private vineyard. The Piedmont Seniors saw a pincushion of Adolph Hitler and a tall gold ashtray with a swastika on its base, which someone anonymously left at the museum’s door. The museum also has a painting of Lenin that hangs above the reception desk, which the Aretons discovered at a flea market in an abandoned soccer stadium in Warsaw. The best part of the visit was Mr. Areton’s infectious enthusiasm about his collection. He told the group that for propaganda purposes, it was commonplace to show small children on posters to give dictators a gentler appearance and mislead the public. The Areton’s goal is to make the public aware of how we can be influenced by propaganda, how to recognize propaganda, and then make independent decisions about how to think. There is no admission fee at the museum, but the Aretons gratefully accept donations. The museum is located at 1000 Fifth Street in San Rafael. The Areton’s “real job” is organizing a large student exchange program through Cultural Homestay International. The museum has limited hours Thursday through Saturday in the afternoons, or by special appointment. The Piedmont Seniors then enjoyed a nice luncheon in downPiedmont Seniors: (front) Janet Epstein (left), Penny Robb, Sue Getreuer, Mona Jamieson, Elizabeth Wierzbianska; (back) Jim Ayotte, Gregory Jurin, Susan McCreary, Museum curator Tom Areton, and Cheryl Stanton. town San Rafael at “Bogies, Too,” which displays various pictures of Humphrey Bogart in his numerous films. After lunch the Piedmont Seniors front of Mission Arcángel in San Rafael. A poster at the Museum of International Propaganda shows Joseph Stalin in his glorified military uniform holding a baby (symbolizing the future) to show his humanity. group visited “Art Works Downtown”, a variety of art galleries conveniently located next to the restaurant. These galleries are run by independent local artists and include beautiful jewelry, paintings, and crafts. The last stop of the day was a visit to Mission Arcángel, a focal point in San Rafael. It was founded as a hospital to treat sick Native Americans in 1817. The mission served as Alta California’s first sanitarium, therefore was called the “Angel of Bodily Healing.” It received full mission status in 1822 from the Roman Catholic Church. Unfortunately, the hospital and much of the property no longer exists, but services in the two chapels take place every week.

articles.text: It’s one thing to ask for a little help with daily activities in the home, but getting 24-hour care can be intimidating at first. Around-the-clock care can be needed for the following reasons: • Post-surgery recovery • Support of hospice and palliative care • Chronic conditions such as dementia that may include symptoms such as wandering • Increased fall risk A trained caregiver can help with bathing assistance, grooming, meal preparation, toileting, medication reminders, transportation to medical appointments, and more when 24-hour care is needed. Whatever the need, there are benefits to receiving 24-hour care in the home for yourself or a loved, either temporarily or for an extended period of time: 1. Family caregivers can get much-needed rest when there is a professional caregiver as part of the team. This is called Respite Care, and it allows friends and family to take care of themselves when a loved needs overnight care as well as daytime assistance. As the saying goes, “You can’t pour from an empty cup,” and a caregiver cannot truly be helpful if they are not getting good sleep and exercise to recharge. 2. When someone becomes more confined to their home due to age or illness, a companion caregiver can lift their spirits. Loneliness does not need to be added to illness and people can truly benefit from a kind smile and friendly conversation. There can be give and take in a care partnership, where someone who is in need of care can still feel valued and share their experiences and knowledge with their caregiver. 3. Call it peace of mind, being reassured, having a safety plan, whatever you prefer, but it comes down to the fact that a compassionate and trained caregiver can provider more security. Illness and age can create vulnerability and someone who is in a weaker condition may need the eyes, ears, and extra set of hands for improved well-being. A falls risk assessment in the home can help to determine how simple changes can be made to make the environment safer for everyone involved in care. 4. When someone is transitioning from a hospital to home or from a rehabilitation center to home, it can be reassuring to have a caregiver who is with them through all of it. This caregiver can observe any changes and share concerns with the family to communicate to the health care provider. 5. Something as simple as making sure medications are taken at the correct times and doses can be the difference between a trajectory of getting better or being readmitted to the hospital. A caregiver can stay on top of medication reminders as well as meal preparation to encourage noticeable improvements. 6. Not all forms of care can come to the home so that’s why it’s beneficial to have a reliable caregiver who can provide transportation to and from medical appointments, whether to a physical therapist or the primary care provider. In order to fully heal, follow-up appointments and adherence to prescribed therapies are critical. If any of these needs ring true, 24-hour care might benefit you and your family. Homewatch CareGivers is locat­ ed at 3820 Broadway in Oakland and is owned and operated by Piedmon­ ters Benjamin and Leah Bloom. You can reach them at 835-9362 or find them at www.CarePiedmont.com. 4. On password management software like 1Password, or LastPass. These are my choice, since they offer the opportunity to create “family vaults”. In the case of 1Password, you can add another “family organizer” so they have access to your account in case you can’t sign in or pass away. LastPass also has levels of access that you can allow other users. What about accessing your iPhone and iPad? Apple has finally provided a new feature in the soon to be released iOS 15.2 for your iPhone and iPad, that promises help for family members trying to wrestle with your data after you are gone. As of this new update (to be released sometime soon), you will be able to add Legacy Contacts, trusted people who can access your Apple ID and your devices in the event of your death. After providing a death certificate, these contacts will be provided an access key to download all your data. Of course, this will include everything, so make sure you really trust them! As our lives become more technically involved, so must our preparation for access to this technology postmortem. And as one who has struggled to settle the estate of a loved one, and been frustrated with no access to necessary passwords for the countless accounts we had to close, I have become committed to making sure my own family will have an easier time after I am gone. articles.text: It’s no secret that when a new baby joins a family, every member’s role shifts a bit. Or a lot. Depending on the family structure and its history of interaction, the transformation of your role as Parent to that of Grandparent may suit you to a T, or may be a rather difficult adjustment. With communication and compromise, finding the right balance is possible. The clock starts ticking as soon as you learn that your adult child or their partner is pregnant. During this time, the young parents-to-be are going through a whirlwind of preparations for themselves; they wonder if their baby will be healthy, how they will manage work issues, housing, childcare, and wonder if they will succeed at being parents. For the expectant grandparents, a different set of questions may arise, mainly because Grandparenthood is a role that is awarded through a life event happening to their child, and its timing is out of the grandparents’ control. A grandparent-to-be may wonder: • Do I live close enough to the young family to be involved regularly? • If so, will the parents want my involvement, and if so how much? • Am I physically fit enough for childcare? For a newborn? A busy toddler? • Do I have time in my personal life to devote to the young family’s day-to-day life, and do I have the desire? • What kind of grandparent have I imagined myself to be? • Does my vision sync with the vision and expectation that the parents have for me? What if they want more or less input from me? • How will I react if my vision of the grandparent role differs from the parents’? It can be hard to predict what a young family may need once a baby is born. It may be that the parents are well-prepared and invite you to participate at any level that you desire. For a first baby, the parents may simply be exhausted from lack of sleep and any help you can provide will be welcome. If the baby is the second or third child, all the issues get more complicated, and the parents may desire your help more and more. Finding balance as a grandparent is at least two-fold: discovering what feels right for you, and learning what will suit your adult children’s expectations. You’ll want to find a comfortable role for yourself, one that is compatible with the vision you have always had for what you’ll be like as a grandparent. Take a look at your life and your future, and think about how you may be able to incorporate your growing grandchildren into that life, while continuing to find personal satisfaction in other areas of life that you enjoy. Your adult children may have their own hopes and dreams for what kind of grandparents they will have in their life. They may remember their own grandparents and want something that is the same – or very different. They may need lots of help with childcare and finances, or they may want absolutely no input. Like all the other important issues that arise in your family, this new journey to grandparenthood will benefit from communication. The best time to talk things through with your adult children is before the baby is born, even though there is still so much unknown. Talk honestly about how you think you will thrive best as a new grandparent. Let the young adults know what level of involvement you are hoping for, so that they are neither overwhelmed with your input nor disappointed in your remoteness. In any growing family, each member may have their own set of expectations and capabilities as their role changes. Uniting the two generations’ vision of shared family life is the goal. For grandparents, finding the right balance as you approach this important stage of life is a team effort. Cynthia Kane is a board-certified, licensed genetic counselor with 25 years of clinical experience. A grandmother, Cynthia has a certificate in Grandfamily Leadership and is the founder of It’s Their Turn, which provides counseling, support, and education for grandparents. Online Grandparent Groups are forming now. Her website, https://itstheirturn.com/, provides a wealth of information and resources for grandparents. Cynthia can be reached at cynthia@itstheirturn.com
articles.title: Finding the right balance as a grandparent

articles.text: Computer tips and helpful suggestions, especially for people who are not entirely comfortable using their computers. Dear Macmama: My wife and I just updated our will and trust, but I feel like I should make other preparations. For example, should I give my passwords to my kids, so they can access my computer when I pass away? Allen P., Oakland Dear Allen: The more that you can prepare your family members for the event of your passing, the easier time they will have with the immense work involved in settling an estate. I know that most of us work hard to make sure we have all our financial affairs in order so our beneficiaries will have an easier time when we pass, but there are so many things in our digital life that we don’t think of. One of my nephews, who works in cyber security says that each person should create a digital “If I Go Missing” folder that contains all our important passwords and phone numbers. Things like our email passwords, credit card and bank passwords, airlines, shopping and Apple ID to name a few. If you just examine your daily routine, you will be amazed at how many times you must sign in or authenticate to access an account, a website, a subscription or your bank. It’s a good idea to take notes for a week or so, to determine what to add to this folder or document. Now comes the tricky part. If you have a document or a spreadsheet with all this vital information, where can you keep it securely and away from hackers or thieves? Here are a few possibilities: 1. On a piece of paper in a safe. As long as you give the combination to your home safe and let your family members know that this document is there, it’s as safe as anything in your home. Which is to say, it can be stolen or broken into, but still better than in a drawer in your desk. 2. A document on your computer. This is the most common solution and can be encrypted with a password. Again, you must let your family members know how to get into your computer and where this document is stored. But this is not the best solution, as it’s not very secure and often difficult to access when you are not present. 3. In a Google Doc. I know that many folks keep private info in a Google document, limiting access by only sharing access with family members. Google’s servers are as secure as most cloud suites, but not meant for ultra-secure data. This also has setbacks, not so much because there is a security issue, but there is too much room for user error.
articles.title: Including computer password in a Will?

articles.text: Editor: It is a pleasure for us to endorse Betsy Smegal Andersen for a second term on the City Council. We have known Betsy for most of her life and have watched with the utmost of admiration the progression of her education, career, and public service. Most recently, as a member of the City Council we have observed her gift for bringing consensus to the community around the issues of the new pool complex. She was not just a speaking proponent of the proposal, but she also visited community members directly impacted by the construction and installation of the pool to seek their input and address their concerns. She did this in addition to collecting information from the community as a whole as to the use and impact of the pool comThis is just one example of the care and thought she puts into issues that involve our City. Another thing that we admire about Betsy, in this turbulent time, is her style and grace. She is obviously well-prepared for this job by her education and on-thejob experience, but she is never combative. We have watched her sit quietly through some explosive issues and then respond in a thoughtful and respectful manner once again in an attempt to bring consensus to issues before the Council. It is our hope that you will join us and vote for Betsy on November 8. She is someone who takes responsibility seriously and someone who will bring respect to the table. –John and Carolee Morrison
articles.title: Vote for Betsy Andersen – an experienced consensus builder

articles.text: The following letter was sent to the City Council and Public Works Director Editor: While street sweeping is conducted by a Public Works Department professional driving a very expensive street sweeping machine, our city’s street sweeping program is run like an amateur volunteer activity. Effective street sweeping requires that the machine sweeps up fallen leaves in the gutters, otherwise those leaves wash down into our storm drains and clog them. Yet, cars routinely park on streets scheduled for sweeping, so the machine just sweeps around them, missing most of the gutter leaves. Why do cars remain on streets during sweeping days? The answer is because clearing the streets depends upon an intensive and frustrating volunteer effort. Local residents have to find out and remember when their street is scheduled for sweeping. Then, volunteer residents have to tie or tape cardboard “no parking” signs to trees or poles in front of their houses. Then, they have to call the Public Works Department to report that they have mounted the temporary signs. And the report must be made three full days before the scheduled street sweeping day. On the street sweeping day, the volunteer has to see if any cars are parked where the signs were posted, and if so, call the Piedmont Police to report a violation. Then they have to wait to see if a cop will come out to ticket the violating parker. Whew! Most neighbors don’t have time to actually go through this process. Last year my wife followed the city protocol to the letter because a lot of leaves had been accumulating. She raked the leaves away from the gutter into the street to help the machine collect them. In spite of her efforts, four cars parked on the street, ignoring the signs she posted. This is not the way to run a professional city service, and, the lack of adequate sweeping costs our city extra expense to clean out clogged storm drains. The solution is not rocket science; it just requires looking at what most other cities do. Then, volunteer residents have to tie or tape cardboard “no parking” signs to trees or poles in front of their houses. Then, they have to call the Public Works Department to report that they have mounted the temporary signs. And the report must be made three full days before the scheduled street sweeping day. On the street sweeping day, the volunteer has to see if any cars are parked where the signs were posted, and if so, call the Piedmont Police to report a violation. Then they have to wait to see if a cop will come out to ticket the violating parker. Whew! Most neighbors don’t have time to actually go through this process. Last year my wife followed the city protocol to the letter because a lot of leaves had been accumulating. She raked the leaves away from the gutter into the street to help the machine collect them. In spite of her efforts, four cars parked on the street, ignoring the signs she posted. This is not the way to run a professional city service, and, the lack of adequate sweeping costs our city extra expense to clean out clogged storm drains. The solution is not rocket science; it just requires looking at what most other cities do. Sudoku Solution SUDOKU SOLUTION (1) Post permanent signs saying “No Parking” on those specific dates and times. (2) Deploy police to enforce the regularly scheduled “no parking” rules. (3) Empower the street sweeping machine operator to report parkers to the police, for ticketing. This is similar to the way Oakland conducts its street sweeping parking restrictions on streets adjacent to Piedmont, including Linda and Kingston. It is long past time for Piedmont to run its street sweeping operation professionally. Taxpayers paid a lot of money for the street sweeping machines, and that money is wasted if the machine can’t clean the gutters due to cars parked on designated sweeping days. Please implement these suggestions and run our City maintenance program professionally. – Bruce Joffe Thanks to Harvest Festival volunteers Editor: A big thank you to the organizers and participants in this year’s Harvest Festival! For backyard growers, the rain was welcome, however, plans had to be changed. I want to recognize the folks who worked on preparing this event. The Piedmont Recreation Department did a great job in creating the event – special thanks to Eva Phalen and Liam Kelly. Andrea Horvath from the Piedmont Education Foundation organized the carnival with Amber Brumfiel in charge of the scarecrows. Volunteers Greg Slatoff, Carolyn George and Jane Reed were in charge of the music, edible contest judges and art show. Thank you for your years of leadership in the Harvest Festival. The Village Market provided the prize for the Sweepstakes Award for the person who entered the most categories. ACE Garden Center donated the Bill Drum Award for the entrant with the most blue ribbons. The edibles contest was held in the Community Hall as usual. Thank you for being a part of a wet Harvest Festival. –Susan Hill Susan Hill is co-founder with the late Bill Drum of the annual Piedmont Harvest Festival. Vote for Betsy Andersen – an experienced consensus builder Editor: It is a pleasure for us to endorse Betsy Smegal Andersen for a second term on the City Council. We have known Betsy for most of her life and have watched with the utmost of admiration the progression of her education, career, and public service. Most recently, as a member of the City Council we have observed her gift for bringing consensus to the community around the issues of the new pool complex. She was not just a speaking proponent of the proposal, but she also visited community members directly impacted by the construction and installation of the pool to seek their input and address their concerns. She did this in addition to collecting information from the community as a whole as to the use and impact of the pool complex. This is just one example of the care and thought she puts into issues that involve our City. Another thing that we admire about Betsy, in this turbulent time, is her style and grace. She is obviously well-prepared for this job by her education and on-thejob experience, but she is never combative. We have watched her sit quietly through some explosive issues and then respond in a thoughtful and respectful manner once again in an attempt to bring consensus to issues before the Council. It is our hope that you will join us and vote for Betsy on November 8. She is someone who takes responsibility seriously and someone who will bring respect to the table. –John and Carolee Morrison Why I’m voting for Jennifer Long Editor: When I moved to Piedmont a few years ago, our family made a commitment to plant our roots here because of the schools and the ability to build a community in a smaller town. Residents have pushed the city to provide more accessibility with City officials. “We are so glad you are here and we so need your services,” said Mayor Teddy Gray King at the council meeting. “We dreamed about you,” added Council member Conna McCarthy. “Yes, for years,” Mayor King confirmed. “Expectations have grown. People used to just get news from local newspapers. Now they [also] want direct contact with the city,” said Schneider. Five years ago, the City of Berkeley created its version of the position, titled Digital Communications Coordinator. Schneider was the first to be hired. She developed Berkeley’s program, which has grown to a staff of four. When the pandemic hit she was appointed as Manager of COVID- 19 communications for Berkeley’s Public Health Department. “Echa comes to Piedmont with deep experience in local government,” said Piedmont City Administrator Sara Lillevand. “She led the internal and external COVID-19 communications for Berkeley’s Public Health Department and city-wide pandemic response. Think about that for a moment, because that’s not what she signed up for, that’s not the job she originally took.” The Piedmont job posting listed the following duties for the new position: • Plan, organize, and execute comprehensive communications and public outreach programs for the City. • Develop Citywide strategic and ongoing communications, social media, branding, and media efforts. • Prepare a variety of written, oral, and multimedia communications. • Provide complex and responsible support to the City Clerk. • Supervise the operations and staff of KCOM, the city government access television station. Among her many new responsibilities Schneider understands that housing in Piedmont and the Regional Housing Needs Allocation (RHNA) will be a major issue. “Development is controversial everywhere. [Berkeley and Oakland] have had more time, 10-15 years, to discuss [the development of housing]. The hard conversations about development are newer here in Piedmont,” she explained. Schneider discovered a passion for city politics while reporting on Oakland city government for Oak Book and SFGate. Schneider has lived in Oakland for 20 years, founded and operated an award-winning local blog called “A Better Oakland” from 2007-2011. It covered Oakland City Council meetings and policy. “[The site] started off as my way to get my opinion out there, and that evolved into writing straight news articles,” she explained. Schneider will also look to improve the City’s website. She designed and launched the Oakland Public Library’s website in 2011, a design which served the library for over 10 years. Schneider will receive general direction from City Clerk John Tulloch.
